3.4 Derive an expression that relates the dissolved oxygen concentration in water (expressed as $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) to the volume in $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of thiosulphate added at the endpoint. Determine that concentration for the water tested.

Deduce the volume of oxygen (in $\mathrm{cm^3}$), determined at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and at a pressure of $101{,}325\,\mathrm{Pa}$, contained in a litre of water (measured at ambient temperature). Give the temperature of the water.

problems.title: Kinetics of an SN1 Reaction
problems.problem:
Practical problem 4. Kinetics of an $\mathrm{S_N1}$ Reaction

In an aqueous ethanolic solution, tert-butyl chloride (2-chloro-2-methylpropane) undergoes an $\mathrm{S_N1}$ nucleophilic substitution reaction leading to the formation of 2-methylpropan-2-ol and hydrochloric acid:

$$\textit{tert}\text{-}\ce{BuCl + H2O} = \textit{tert}\text{-}\ce{BuOH + HCl}$$

The rate of the reaction is given by

$$\frac{d[\ce{HCl}]}{dt} = k_1\,[\textit{tert}\ \ce{BuCl}]$$

The aim of this experiment is to determine the rate constant $k_1$ at ambient temperature.

Procedure:

1. Using a pipette transfer $2.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of tert-butyl chloride (flask 4.1 on the general-use bench) into a clean and dry $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ ground neck Erlenmeyer (conical) flask.
2. As soon as possible add $148\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ (measure with the graduated cylinder) of the aqueous ethanol solution standing on the general-use bench (flask 4.2).
3. Stopper the Erlenmeyer flask and stir vigorously using the magnetic stirrer. Start your timer. Note carefully the temperature, $T(0)$, of the solution.
4. After approximately 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, 55 min (determined accurately), transfer $10.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ samples using a pipette into $20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of a mixture of ice and acetone (propanone). Add 2 drops of bromothymol blue and titrate the liberated acid with a solution of $Y\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ aqueous sodium hydroxide ($Y$ will be shown on the board).

Questions:

4.1 The concentrations of tert-BuCl at time $t = 0$ and at time $t$ are linked by the following relationship:

$$\ln\frac{[\mathrm{tertBuCl}]_0}{[\mathrm{tertBuCl}]_t} = k_1 . t$$

Establish the theoretical expression:

$$\ln\frac{V_\infty}{V_\infty - V} = k_1\,t$$

where $V$ stands for the volume of sodium hydroxide used at time $t$ and $V(\infty)$ for the corresponding value at $t(\infty)$.

$$t_\infty = t(\infty);\quad V_\infty = V(\infty)$$

4.2 Calculate $V(\infty)$ (density of tert-BuCl at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $850\,\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, molar mass of tert-BuCl: $92.5\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$).

4.3 Fill in the table on the answer sheet whose columns will be:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} t\,(\mathrm{min}) & V\,(\mathrm{cm^3}) & V_\infty & V & \dfrac{V_\infty}{V_\infty - V} & \ln\dfrac{V_\infty}{V_\infty - V} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

Draw the curve

$$\ln\frac{V_\infty}{V_\infty - V} = f(t)$$

4.4 Determine the value of $k_1$ (give the value of $t(0)$).

problems.title: Determination of an acid dissociation constant
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1. Determination of an acid dissociation constant [printed as Problem 1 (Practical); no points or weight are printed in the source]

Reagents:

• A solution of a weak monoprotic acid with a concentration of about $0.1\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$,
• a solution of sodium hydroxide with a concentration of about $0.1\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$,
• solutions of the indicators: methyl orange and phenolphthalein.

Equipment:

• burette $25\,\mathrm{cm^3}$,
• calibrated pipette $20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$,
• two conical flasks $200\,\mathrm{cm^3}$,
• access to the $pH$-meter. An assistant will make one measurement only for each participant.

Questions:

1.1 Give the expression for the concentration dissociation constant of the acid HA.

1.2 Give your reasons for the choice of the indicator.

1.3 Give the results of titrations.

1.4 Write down your $pH$ value (measured by assistant).

1.5 Show how you calculate the concentration $pK_a$ value for the acid. Write down the value.

problems.title: Determination of the formation (stability) constants of the complex ions [Cu(NH3)4]2+ and [Zn(NH3)4]2+
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2. Determination of the formation (stability) constants of the complex ions $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ and $\ce{[Zn(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ [printed as Problem 2 (Practical); no points or weight are printed in the source]

Equipment:

• Two dry beakers with copper and zinc electrodes,
• three bottles with aqueous solutions of $\ce{CuSO4}$, $\ce{ZnSO4}$ and $\ce{NH3}$, respectively,
• one beaker with strips of filter paper for making a salt bridge,
• one beaker with an aqueous solution of $\ce{KNO3}$,
• three pipettes for delivering $\ce{CuSO4}$, $\ce{ZnSO4}$ and $\ce{NH3}$ solutions,
• digital voltmeter for the EMF measurements,
• red and blue leads (conductors) for connecting cell electrodes to the digital voltmeter,
• rubber pipette filler,
• appropriately marked glass stirring rods.

a) Procedure for setting up the Daniell cell:

1. Into the dry beakers containing Cu and Zn electrodes deliver $20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{CuSO4}$ and $20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{ZnSO4}$ using marked pipettes in order to get $\ce{Cu/Cu^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Zn/Zn^{2+}}$ half-cells.
2. Wet the filter paper strip with $\ce{KNO3}$ solution. The strip should only be moisten with the solution. Then place the strip ends into the $\ce{CuSO4}$ and $\ce{ZnSO4}$ solutions.
3. Connect the leads to the electrodes (red to Cu electrode and blue to Zn electrode).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1991-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1

b) Procedure for the EMF measurement of the Daniell cell ($E_\mathrm{A}$):

Put the appropriately marked glass rods (red - Cu, blue - Zn) into the $\ce{CuSO4}$ and $\ce{ZnSO4}$ solutions. Having stirred the solutions gently with the rods, the rods should be left in the solutions throughout the course of the experiment. Start the EMF measurement of the cell by connecting the red lead to the voltmeter terminal (HI) and the blue one to the negative terminal (LO). If the EMF value changes by no more than $0.001\,\mathrm{V}$, record the EMF ($E_\mathrm{A}$).

c) Procedure for the EMF measurement of the cell ($E_\mathrm{B}$) after the addition of the complexing agent ($\ce{NH3}$ solution) into the $\ce{Cu/Cu^{2+}}$ half-cell:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1991-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2

Pipette $20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of aqueous $\ce{NH3}$ solution into the $\ce{CuSO4}$ solution. Stir the solution with a glass rod gently until it becomes a clear dark blue. Leave the rod in the solution. Measure and record the new EMF ($E_\mathrm{B}$), in the way described in part b).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1991-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3

d) Procedure for the EMF measurement of the cell ($E_\mathrm{C}$) after the addition of the complexing agent ($\ce{NH3}$ solution) to the $\ce{Zn/Zn^{2+}}$ half-cell:

Leave the $\ce{Cu/[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ half-cell unchanged. Add $20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{NH3}$ solution to the $\ce{ZnSO4}$ half-cell. Carry out the EMF measurement of the cell in the way described in part b). Write down the result ($E_\mathrm{C}$).

Theoretical considerations:

Gas constant $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$

Faraday constant $F = 96\,487\,\mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}$

i) The concentrations of $\ce{CuSO4}$, $\ce{ZnSO4}$ and $\ce{NH3}$ aqueous solutions written on the bottles are expressed in $\mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}$. Therefore they must be converted into appropriate concentrations expressed in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$. The densities ($d$) of the solutions as functions of temperature are respectively:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{CuSO4}: & d_1 = 1.0923\ (\mathrm{kg\,dm^{-3}}) - 0.0002700\ (\mathrm{kg\,dm^{-3}\,K^{-1}})\ T \\ \ce{ZnSO4}: & d_2 = 1.0993\ (\mathrm{kg\,dm^{-3}}) - 0.0002900\ (\mathrm{kg\,dm^{-3}\,K^{-1}})\ T \\ \ce{NH3}: & d_3 = 1.0740\ (\mathrm{kg\,dm^{-3}}) - 0.0002800\ (\mathrm{kg\,dm^{-3}\,K^{-1}})\ T \end{array}$$

ii) In order to convert concentrations ($c_i$) into ionic activities ($a_i$), we need to calculate activities of the ions using the equation $a_i = f_i \cdot c_i$. The activity coefficient values, $f_i$, of the ions involved are given in the answer sheet. The activity coefficient of ammonia should be assumed to be 1.

iii) To simplify the calculations it should be assumed that after the addition of the excess of complexing agent ($\ce{NH3}$) only $\ce{Cu^{2+}_{aq}}$, $\ce{Zn^{2+}_{aq}}$, $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$, $\ce{[Zn(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ ions exist in the respective solutions.

iv) Any diffusion potential occurring between both half-cells when the salt bridge is applied may be neglected in practice.

Questions:

2.1 Calculate the values of the concentrations of $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Zn^{2+}}$ ions in the Daniell cell before the introduction of the complexing agent ($\ce{NH3}$).

2.2 Calculate the standard EMF value $E^\circ$ of your Daniell cell using the Nernst equation.

2.3 Calculate the concentrations of $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ and $\ce{NH3}$ in the B type cell, i.e. after the addition of $\ce{NH3}$ to the $\ce{Cu/Cu^{2+}}$ half-cell.

2.4 Determine the values of the thermodynamic formation (stability) constants $K_B$ and $\ln K_B$ for the $\ce{[Cu(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ ions.

2.5 Calculate the concentrations of $\ce{[Zn(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ and $\ce{NH3}$ in the type C cell, i. e. after the addition of $\ce{NH3}$ to the $\ce{Zn/Zn^{2+}}$ half-cell.

2.6 Determine the values of the thermodynamic formation (stability) constant $K_C$ and $\ln K_C$ for $\ce{[Zn(NH3)4]^{2+}}$ ions.

problems.title: Effects of CO2 on Solubility
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1. Effects of $\ce{CO2}$ on Solubility

Calcium carbonate is a partially soluble material commonly known as limestone, marble, chalk, or calcite. In the presence of $\ce{CO2}$-rich groundwater, calcium carbonate dissolves to form cavities and caves in limestone formations.

In this experiment you will determine the solubility of calcium carbonate in an aqueuos solution saturated with carbon dioxide and in solution free of carbon dioxide. The $[\ce{Ca^{2+}}]$ will be determined by complexometric titration with EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid).

a) Procedure for the determination of $[\ce{Ca^{2+}}]$

1. Calibrate your $pH$ meter.
2. Measure and record the $pH$ of the sample equilibrated with solid $\ce{CaCO3}$ and $\ce{CO2}$ gas.
3. Filter all your sample into a second $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ plastic bottle to remove any suspended $\ce{CaCO3}$. Quickly cap the bottle when the filtering is complete.
4. Uncap the bottle long enough to measure and record the pH of the filtered solution and recap the bottle until you are ready for the next step.
5. As rapidly as possible, transfer three $25\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquots of this sample to three Erlenmeyer flasks. Recap the sample bottle after removing each $25\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot.
6. Add 15 drops of $6\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$ to each of the three flasks with stirring. Any $\ce{CaCO3}$ that may have formed should dissolve. Before proceeding with the next step, make sure there is no solid $\ce{CaCO3}$ in the Erlenmeyer flasks. If a flask has some solid present, then more stirring is necessary.
7. To one, and only one flask, add $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of a pH 10 $\ce{NH3}$ buffer. Proceed immediately with steps 8 - 10.
8. Add 20 drops of $0.001\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{Mg^{2+}}/\ce{EDTA^{4-}}$ solution to the flask in order for the indicator to function properly.
9. Add 5 drops of Calmagite indicator to the sample.
10. Titrate the sample with an approximately $0.01\,\mathrm{M}$ EDTA solution provided (to be standardized as directed below) to a colour change from red to blue. You may wish to make a reference for colour with water, buffer, two drops EDTA and indicator.
11. Quickly repeat steps 7 - 10 for each remaining flask, one at a time.
12. After steps 1 - 11 have been completed to your satisfaction, transfer the remaining filtered, saturated solution from step 3 to a suitable beaker. Heat this solution to $96 - 99\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and allow it to remain at that temperature, with magnetic stirring, for 5 minutes. A stirrer setting on 6 is adequate, and an initial high setting of heat will be required. You should see $\ce{CO2}$ being evolved and some $\ce{CaCO3}$ may precipitate.
13. At the end of the five minutes heating period, use the beaker tongs to remove the beaker from the hot plate and place it in an ice bath. Allow the solution to cool to room temperature.
14. Measure and record the $pH$ of the cooled solution.
15. Filter the solution to remove any suspended $\ce{CaCO3}$.
16. Transfer three $25\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquots of this filtered solution to three Erlenmeyer flasks. Add about $25\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of deionized water to each flask, followed by 15 drops of $6\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$.
17. Titrate each sample according to steps 7 - 11.

b) Procedure for standardization of EDTA

1. Weigh approximately $0.35\,\mathrm{g}$ of dried primary standard $\ce{CaCO3}$, (molar mass $100.09\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$) which will be found in the weighing bottle in the desiccator. Note: $\ce{CaCO3}$ is hygroscopic.
2. Add $25\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of deionized water to the $\ce{CaCO3}$, then carefully add $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $6\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$. Quickly cover with a watch glass.
3. When the $\ce{CaCO3}$ has dissolved, quantitatively transfer the solution to a $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask and dilute to the mark.
4. Transfer three $25\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquots of the standard $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ solution to three Erlenmeyer flasks.
5. Proceed to titrate each sample according to steps 7 - 11, following each step in sequence.

Tasks:

1.1 Calculate the solubility of calcium carbonate (expressed in $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) in a solution saturated with both $\ce{CaCO3}$ and $\ce{CO2}$ and in solution free of $\ce{CO2}$.

1.2 List all the ionic species that increase in concentration as a result of the dissolving of $\ce{CaCO3}$ in water.

1.3 Given below are brief descriptions of two solutions. Circle the one in which the concentration of $\ce{CO3^{2-}}$ would be highest:

a) a solution produced by dissolving $\ce{CaCO3(s)}$ in $\ce{CO2}$-saturated water
b) a solution produced by dissolving $\ce{CaCO3(s)}$ in $\ce{CO2}$-free water

1.4 Will the solubility of $\ce{CaCO3}$ increase or decrease in a solution from which the $\ce{CO2}$ has been removed?

problems.title: Synthesis
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1. Synthesis [printed as Problem 1 (Practical); no points or weight are printed in the source]

Cholesterol (1) is a natural sterol metabolite present in animal and vegetal organisms. This compound can be oxidized by Jones' reagent into its corresponding 3-ketoderivative (2). The latter, when treated with bases, undergoes isomerization of the carbon-carbon double bond leading to $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone (3).

The conversion of $\Delta^{5}$-3$\beta$-hydroxy steroids into their corresponding $\Delta^{4}$-3-ketones is an important reaction in steroid chemistry and represents the last step of the synthesis of a variety of commercial hormones.

You will be marked for the purity of the product (3).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1993-1-fig1.png

Procedure:

a) Dissolve your pre-weighed sample of cholesterol ($386\,\mathrm{mg}$, $1\,\mathrm{mmol}$) contained in a $50\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ flask A with acetone ($20\,\mathrm{cm^3}$) warming gently the flask in a bath tub of hot water. When the sample is completely dissolved, cool the flask containing the solution to the temperature by cold water.
b) Add dropwise $0.40\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of Jones' reagent to the solution, gently swirling the flask in a bath of cold water. The formation of a green precipitate [$\ce{Cr2(SO4)3}$] is observed during the addition of Jones' reagent.
c) Remove the green precipitate by filtration with paper filter.
d) Add slowly water ($10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$) to the clean filtrate. The ketone (2) begins to precipitate.
e) Filter the precipitate over the Büchner funnel under reduced pressure, washing the crystals with small portions of a 2 : 1 acetone/water mixture.
f) Dissolve the ketone (2) in methanol ($15\,\mathrm{cm^3}$). Add to the solution just one drop of 5 % methanolic $\ce{NaOH}$ solution and warm the mixture in a bath of hot water for 10 min.
g) The $\Delta^{4}$-3-ketosteroid (3) precipitates spontaneously, upon addition of water (ca. $2\,\mathrm{cm^3}$) to the cooled reaction mixture. Filter the crystals over the Büchner funnel under reduced pressure and recrystallize the product by methanol. If you do not get the crystals, add a few drops of water. Remember! You are getting a mark for the purity, not the yield.
h) Dry carefully the crystals on a porous plate. Determine the melting point of the ketone (3) and write its value on your student's report. Taking into account the correction reported on the top of the thermometer (see example at the end).
i) Put the crystals in the plastic vial B, write on it your personal identification number (see the left corner of your badge), and deliver it to one of the supervisors.

The melting point of the ketone (3) will be checked by the lab supervisors.

problems.title: Analysis
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2. Analysis [printed as Problem 2 (Practical); no points or weight are printed in the source]

Citric acid (2-hydroxy-1,2,3-propanetricarboxylic acid) is widely distributed in plants and in animal tissues. Lemon juice contains from 5 to 8% of this acid. It is produced by mycological fermentation on an industrial scale using crude sugar solutions, such as molasses, and stains of Aspergillus niger.

It is utilized as an acidulant and antioxidant in several beverages.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1993-2-fig1.png

a) Standardization of $\ce{NaOH}$ solution (ca $0.1\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) by potassium hydrogen phthalate

Procedure:

A preweighed quantity ($2.050\,\mathrm{g}$) of potassium hydrogen phthalate is in the $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask B. Dilute this sample with water to the mark. Phenolphthalein indicator (2 - 3 drops) is added to an aliquot of $25.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the resulting solution and the solution is then titrated with the $\ce{NaOH}$ solution that has to be standardized.

Give the concentration of the $\ce{NaOH}$ solution.

b) Titrimetric determination of citric acid

Procedure:

The unknown sample of citric acid is in the $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask C. Dilute the sample with water to the mark. Transfer $25.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the resulting solution into a $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ Erlenmeyer flask and dilute with water. Add 2 – 3 drops of phenolphthalein indicator and titrate with the previously standardized $\ce{NaOH}$ solution.

Give the mass of citric acid.

problems.title: Determination of Fatty Acids
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1 (23 blue points, 23 red points). Determination of Fatty Acids [printed as Practical Problem I]

The starch and phenolphtalein indicator are shared between three students. They should be returned immediately after use, and should be handed to the referees to be exchanged if they become contaminated.

A mixture of an unsaturated monoprotic fatty acid and an ethyl ester of a saturated monoprotic fatty acid has been dissolved in ethanol ($2.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of this solution contain a total of $1.00\,\mathrm{g}$ acid plus ester). By titration the acid number$^{1)}$, the saponification number$^{2)}$ and the iodine number$^{3)}$ of the mixture shall be determined. The acid number and the saponification number shall be used to calculate the number of moles of free fatty acid and ester present in $1.00\,\mathrm{g}$ of the sample. The iodine number shall be used to calculate the number of double bonds in the unsaturated fatty acid.

Note: The candidate must be able to carry out the whole exam by using the delivered amount of unknown sample ($12\,\mathrm{mL}$). There will be no supplementation.

$^{1)}$ Acid number: The mass of KOH in milligram that is required to neutralize one gram of the acid plus ester.

$^{2)}$ Saponification number: The mass of KOH in milligram that is required to saponify one gram of the acid plus ester.

$^{3)}$ Iodine number: The mass of iodine (I) in g that is consumed by $100\,\mathrm{g}$ of acid plus ester.

Atomic masses:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \mathrm{I} = 126.90 & \mathrm{O} = 16.00 \\ \mathrm{K} = 39.10 & \mathrm{H} = 1.01 \end{array}$$

1) Determination of the acid number.

Reagents and Apparatus: Unknown sample, $0.1000\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{KOH}$, indicator (phenolphthalein), ethanol/ether (1:1 mixture), buret ($50\,\mathrm{mL}$), erlenmeyer flasks ($3 \times 250\,\mathrm{mL}$), measuring cylinder ($100\,\mathrm{mL}$), graduated pipette ($2\,\mathrm{mL}$), funnel.

Procedure: Pipet out aliquotes ($2.00\,\mathrm{mL}$) from the unknown mixture into erlenmeyer flasks ($250\,\mathrm{mL}$). Add first ca. $100\,\mathrm{mL}$ of an ethanol/ether mixture (1:1) and then add the indicator (5 drops). Titrate the solutions with $0.1000\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{KOH}$.

Calculate the acid number.

2) Determination of the saponification number.

Reagents and Apparatus: Unknown sample, $0.5000\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{KOH}$ in ethanol, $0.1000\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$, indicator (phenolphthalein), volumetric flask ($50\,\mathrm{mL}$), round bottom flask ($250\,\mathrm{mL}$), Liebig condenser, buret ($50\,\mathrm{mL}$), erlenmeyer flasks ($3 \times 250\,\mathrm{mL}$), volumetric pipette ($25\,\mathrm{mL}$), volumetric pipette ($10\,\mathrm{mL}$), graduated pipette ($2\,\mathrm{mL}$), funnel, glass rod. The round bottom flask and Liebig condenser are to be found in the fume hoods.

Procedure: Pipet out a $2.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquote of the unknown sample into a round bottom flask ($250\,\mathrm{mL}$) and add $25.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ $0.5000\,\mathrm{M}$ KOH/EtOH. Reflux the mixture with a heating mantle for 30 min in the fume hood (start the heating with the mantle set to 10, then turn it down to 5 after 7 min.). Bring the flask back to the bench and cool it under tap water. Transfer quantitatively the solution to a $50\,\mathrm{mL}$ volumetric flask and dilute to the mark with a 1:1 mixture of ethanol/water. Take out aliquots of $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ and titrate with $0.1000\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$ using phenolphtalein as indicator (5 drops).

Calculate the saponification number.

3) Determination of the iodine number.

In this experiment iodobromine adds to the double bond.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1994-1-fig1.png

The Hanus solution ($\ce{IBr}$ in acetic acid) is added in excess. After the reaction is complete, excess iodobromine is reacted with iodide forming $\ce{I2}$, $\ce{IBr + I- -> I2 + Br-}$, which in turn is determined by standard thiosulphate titration.

Warning: Be careful when handling the iodobromine solution. Treat any spill immediately with thiosulphate solution.

Reagents and Apparatus: Unknown sample, $0.2000\,\mathrm{M}$ Hanus solution, dichloro-methane, 15% $\ce{KI}$ solution in distilled water, distilled water, $0.2000\,\mathrm{M}$ sodium thiosulfate, starch indicator, erlenmeyer flasks ($3 \times 500\,\mathrm{mL}$), buret ($50\,\mathrm{mL}$), graduated pipette ($2\,\mathrm{mL}$), measuring cylinders ($10$ and $100\,\mathrm{mL}$), volumetric pipette ($25\,\mathrm{mL}$), aluminium foil.

Procedure: Pipet out aliquotes ($1.00\,\mathrm{mL}$) of the unknown mixture into erlenmeyer flasks ($500\,\mathrm{mL}$) and add $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ of dichloromethane. With a pipet add $25.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ Hanus solution, cover the opening with aluminiumfoil and place your labelled flasks in the dark in the cupboard (under the fume hood) for 30 min. with occasionally shaking. Add $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the 15% $\ce{KI}$ solution, shake thoroughly and add $100\,\mathrm{mL}$ of dist. water. Titrate the solution with $0.2000\,\mathrm{M}$ sodium thiosulphate until the solution turns pale yellow. Add starch indicator ($3\,\mathrm{mL}$) and continue titration until the blue colour entirely disappears.

Calculate the iodine number.

4) Use the results from 1) 2) and 3) to:

i) Calculate the amount of ester (in mol) in $1\,\mathrm{g}$ of the acid plus ester

ii) Calculate the number of double bonds in the unsaturated acid

problems.title: Volumetric Determination of Bromide by Back-Titration with Thiocyanate after Precipitation with Silver Ions in Excess
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2 (17 blue points, 17 red points). Volumetric Determination of Bromide by Back-Titration with Thiocyanate after Precipitation with Silver Ions in Excess [printed as Practical Problem II]

Moments worth considering:

• The candidates must consider the number of significant figures that will be reasonable in the results.
• The candidates must be able to carry out the whole analysis by using the delivered portions of silver nitrate and potassium thiocyanate. Supplementation of these two solutions will not be available.
• Only one $25\,\mathrm{mL}$ pipette will be at disposal for each candidate.

Principle

Bromide is precipitated as silver bromide after a known amount of silver ions has been added in excess.

$$\ce{Ag+(aq) + Br-(aq) -> AgBr(s)} \qquad \text{(faint yellow-green)}$$

The excess of silver ions is titrated with thiocyanate with a known concentration, after a previous standardization of the thiocyanate solution.

During the titration of the following reaction takes place, resulting in the precipitation of silver thiocyanate:

$$\ce{Ag+(aq) + SCN-(aq) -> AgSCN(s)} \qquad \text{(white)}$$

Fe(III) is added as indicator producing a red-coloured ion at the equivalence point:

$$\ce{Fe^{3+}(aq) + SCN-(aq) -> FeSCN^{2+}(aq)} \qquad \text{(red)}$$

a) Procedures

Every candidate has got a $0.5$ liter brown bottle with screw cap, containing about $0.08\,\mathrm{M}$ of a potassium thiocyanate solution, and also a $0.25$ liter brown bottle with screw cap, containing the silver nitrate solution. The concentration of this solution is $0.1000\,\mathrm{M}$. The exact concentration of the $\ce{KSCN}$ solution is to be determined by the candidates.

i) Determination of bromide in the unknown sample solution

Fill the $250\,\mathrm{mL}$ volumetric flask containing the bromide sample solution to the mark with water.

Transfer three $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ portions (pipette) of the sample solution to three erlenmeyer flasks. Add about $5\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $6\,\mathrm{M}$ nitric acid (measuring cylinder) to each flask.

Transfer $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ (pipette) of the accurately known silver solution and about $1\,\mathrm{mL}$ of iron(III) indicator (ind.) (measuring cylinder) to each solution.

Titrate the contents of the three aliquotes with the potassium thioscyanate solution. The end-point of the titration is detected when the solution (including the precipitate) becomes permanently very faint brownish. It is important to shake the contents vigorously near the end-point and rinse the walls of the flask with water. The colour should be stable for at least one minute.

ii) Standardization of the potassium thiocyanate solution:

Transfer $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ (pipette) of the silver nitrate solution to an erlenmeyer flask, add about $5\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $6\,\mathrm{M}$ nitric acid and about $1\,\mathrm{mL}$ of the iron(III) indicator solution and about $25\,\mathrm{mL}$ of water (use measuring cylinders for these solutions).

Titrate the contents with the thiocyannate solution and determine the end-point according to the instruction given in the "Determination" procedure.

Atomic mass: Br = 79.90

b) Exercise

At the equivalent point the solution is saturated with respect to both AgBr and AgSCN. Find the molar consentration of free (unprecipitated) $\ce{Br-}$ in this solution:

$$K_{\mathrm{sp(AgBr)}} = 5.00\cdot10^{-13} \qquad K_{\mathrm{sp(AgSCN)}} = 1.00\cdot10^{-12}$$

Ignore the effect of pH and Fe(III) species.

Note: On the answer sheet, not only the required final results shall be given, but also examplifications of how the calculations are carried out.

problems.title: Identification of Unknown Solutions
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1. Identification of Unknown Solutions

You are supplied with five different solutions contained in five test tubes labelled as A, B, C, D and E, respectively. The solution in each test tube contains one of the following compounds:

$\ce{NH4Cl}$ $\quad$ $\ce{(NH4)2SO4}$ $\quad$ $\ce{NaNO3}$ $\quad$ $\ce{MgCl2}$ $\quad$ $\ce{Na2SO4}$

Identify these solutions.

Reagents

$$\begin{array}{ll} \ce{H2SO4}\ \text{(conc.)} & \ce{H2SO4}\ (6\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}) \\ \ce{HNO3}\ \text{(conc.)} & \ce{HNO3}\ (6\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}) \\ \ce{HCl}\ \text{(conc.)} & \ce{HCl}\ (6\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}) \\ \ce{Ba(OH)2}\ \text{(satd.)} & \ce{NaOH}\ (6\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}) \\ \ce{BaCl2}\ (0.5\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}) & \ce{Ba(NO3)2}\ (0.5\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}) \end{array}$$

NOTES:
(1) You can only select the provided reagents and use a procedure as simple as possible to complete your task. You are getting a mark not only according to the correct identification, but also to the number of steps you have taken.
(2) You have to carry out the whole analysis by using the provided amount of these unknown solutions. Supplement of them will be available, but it will reduce the mark you obtain.

problems.title: Preparation of cis-Copper-bis-Glycinate Hydrate [Cu(gly)2•xH2O]
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2. Preparation of cis-Copper-bis-Glycinate Hydrate [$\ce{Cu(gly)2}\cdot x\ce{H2O}$]

Copper(II) amino acidate coordination compounds are monometric units for synthesizing important biopolymers such as metalloenzymes like ceruloplasmin, on which every living organism depends. In laboratory cis-copper-bis-glycinate hydrate can be produced by the reaction of cupric hydroxide with glycine at a temperature of ca. $70\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Reagents:
• $\ce{CuSO4}\cdot 5\,\ce{H2O(s)}$
• $\ce{NH3(aq)}$ $(3\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})$
• glycine(s)
• 95% ethanol,
• acetone
• $\ce{NaOH}$ $(2\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})$
• $\ce{BaCl2}$ $(0.5\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})$

1. Preparation of $\ce{Cu(OH)2}$

Procedure:
(1) Dissolve your pre-weighted sample of $\ce{CuSO4}\cdot 5\,\ce{H2O}$ $(6.0\,\mathrm{g})$ in $40\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water with a $250\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ beaker as a container.
(2) Add slowly $3\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ ammonia solution to the $\ce{CuSO4}$ solution, gently stirring, until the precipitate is completely dissolved and the solution is turning blue-violet.
(3) Add $2\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ $\ce{NaOH}$ solution to the above solution until no more precipitate formed.
(4) Filter the precipitate over a Büchner funnel under reduced pressure. Wash the precipitate with water until no $\ce{SO4^2-}$ ion is detected in the filtrate.
(5) Collect $\ce{Cu(OH)2}$ for the preparation of $\ce{Cu(gly)2}\cdot x\,\ce{H2O}$.

Write the equations for the main chemical reactions having taken place in the above procedure.

2. Preparation of cis-Copper-bis-Glycinate Hydrate

Procedure:
(1) Dissolve a pre-weighted sample of glycine $(3.6\,\mathrm{g})$ in $130\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water and then warm the solution in a hot water bath $(70\,^\circ\mathrm{C})$. Add the $\ce{Cu(OH)2}$ to the solution, stir gently until the precipitate is dissolved. Perform a hot filtration and add $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 95 % ethanol.
(2) Cool the solution and when needle-like crystals appear, place it in the ice water bath for 10 min.
(3) Filter the crystals over a Büchner funnel under reduced pressure, wash once with $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol-water mixing solvent and then twice with $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ acetone, squeeze the crystals as dry as possible on the funnel.
(4) Collect the crystals to a watch glass and dry it (consult your supervisor).
(5) Half an hour later weigh the product. Write the mass of product and the percentage of yield on your student's report. Give the expressions for calculation to show how you calculate.

[The compendium's solution section lists what had to be written on the answer sheet (the answer sheet itself is not reproduced); the lists are given here without any answers:]
• Mass of the product.
• The calculated theoretical yield in g.
• The yield obtained as a percentage of the theoretical yield.

Tasks:

Write down the balanced chemical equations used in the preparation.

problems.title: Determination of Copper(II) Content in Cu(gly)2 . x H2O
problems.problem:
Practical problem 3. Determination of Copper(II) Content in $\ce{Cu(gly)2}\cdot x\,\ce{H2O}$

The Cu(II) content in $\ce{Cu(gly)2}\cdot x\,\ce{H2O}$ crystals prepared yourself can be determined by iodometry with starch solution as indicator. Based on the data obtained one can calculate the moles of hydrate in $\ce{Cu(gly)2}\cdot x\,\ce{H2O}$.

Reagents:
• Standard $\ce{KIO3}$ (see the label on the bottle to get the accurate concentration)
• $\ce{H2SO4}$ $(1.0\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})$ as indicator.
• $\ce{KI}$ $(0.6\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})$
• $\ce{KSCN}$ $(2\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})$
• Starch (0.5 %)
• $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ (to be standardized)

1. Standardization of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution

Procedure
(1) Transfer $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of standard $\ce{KIO3}$ solution to an Erlenmeyer flask.
(2) Add $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water, $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{KI}$ solution and $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{H2SO4}$ $(1.0\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})$ to the flask.
(3) Titrate immediately with $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution.
(4) Add $2\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ starch solution when the colour of the titrand turns pale yellow.
(5) Continue titrating until the blue colour of the solution disappears.
(6) Proceed with step (1) – (5) twice parallel.

2. Determination of Cu(II) content in $\ce{Cu(gly)2}\cdot x\ce{H2O}$

(1) Weigh 1.0 – 1.2 g (precision of $\pm 0.0002\,\mathrm{g}$) of $\ce{Cu(gly)2}\cdot x\,\ce{H2O}$ with a dry $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ beaker as the container.
(2) Dissolve it with $40\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water and $8\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{H2SO4}$ $(1.0\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}})$.
(3) Transfer the above solution quantitatively to a $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask and dilute to the mark.
(4) Transfer $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the Cu(II) solution to an Erlenmeyer flask, add $50\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water and $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{KI}$ solution to the flask.
(5) Titrate immediately with standardized $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution.
(6) Add $2\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of starch solution and $3\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{KSCN}$ solution to the flask when the colour of the titrand turns from brown to pale yellow.
(7) Titrate continuously until the blue colour of the solution disappears.
(8) Proceed with steps (4) – (7) twice parallel.

[The compendium's solution section lists what had to be written on the answer sheet and further tasks (the answer sheet itself is not reproduced); the lists are given here without any answers:]

Part 1
• Volumes of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution
• Calculation of the concentration of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution.

Part 2
• Mass of the product.
• Volumes of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution
• Mass % of Cu(II) in $\ce{Cu(gly^-)2}\cdot x\,\ce{H2O}$. Calculation.
• The value of x in the formula of the product. Calculation.

Other Tasks:

1. Write two equations for chemical reactions taking place during the standardization of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution.

2. Write the equation for the reaction between $\ce{Cu^2+}$ and $\ce{I-}$.

problems.title: Iodometric Determination of the Concentration of Copper(II) and Iron(III) in a Sample of Technological Solution
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1. Iodometric Determination of the Concentration of Copper(II) and Iron(III) in a Sample of Technological Solution [printed as Problem 1 (Practical); no points or weight are printed in the source]

Reagents

• $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$, $0.008333\ \mathrm{M}$
• $\ce{KI}$, 20 % by mass.
• $\ce{HCl}$, $1\ \mathrm{M}$
• $\ce{H2SO4}$, $1\ \mathrm{M}$
• $\ce{Na4P2O7}$, 5 % by mass.
• Starch, 1 % by mass.
• $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ (should be standardized)
• The solution to be analyzed in $100\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask.

Procedure

1. Standardization of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution

(1) $10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1\ \mathrm{M}$ solution of $\ce{H2SO4}$ and $2\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of 20 % $\ce{KI}$ solution are placed into an Erlenmeyer flask (the solution remains colourless).
(2) $10.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $\ce{K2Cr2O7}$ solution is added.
(3) The Erlenmeyer flask is covered with a watch glass and kept in a dark place for 3 to 5 min.
(4) $100\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of water is added to the flask.
(5) The mixture is titrated immediately with $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution until the colour of mixture changes to pale yellow. Then 10 drops of starch solution are added. The titration continues until blue colour disappears completely.
(6) It is recommended to repeat the titration (steps 1 through 5) two more times.

Do the following and fill in the answer sheet form

1.1 Write the reactions involved in the procedure of standardization of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution

1.2 Calculate the concentration of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution, and write your calculations.

2. The determination of copper

(1) The solution to be analyzed in a $100\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask is diluted with water to the mark and stirred
(2) A $10.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of the solution is placed into an Erlenmeyer flask.
(3) $20\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of 5 % solution of $\ce{Na4P2O7}$, $7\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1\ \mathrm{M}$ solution of $\ce{HCl}$, and $10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of 20 % solution of $\ce{KI}$ are added. A precipitate may form upon the addition of $\ce{Na4P2O7}$.
(4) The Erlenmeyer flask is covered with a watch glass and left in a dark place for 3 - 5 min.
(5) The mixture is titrated immediately with $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution until the colour of suspension changes to pale yellow. Then, 10 drops of starch solution are added. The titration continues until the colour of suspension becomes clear white.
(6) It is recommended to repeat the titration (steps 2 through 5) two more times.

Do the following and fill in the answer sheet form

1.3 Write the reactions involved in the procedure of determination of $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$ ion.

1.4 Calculate the mass of copper in the solution under analysis, and write your calculations.

3. The determination of total amount of copper and iron

(1) A $10.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of the solution prepared in the item 2(1) is placed into an Erlenmeyer flask.
(2) $2\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1\ \mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$ solution and $10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of 20 % $\ce{KI}$ solution are added.
(3) The Erlenmeyer flask is covered with a watch glass and kept in a dark place for 3 to 5 min.
(4) The mixture is titrated immediately with $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution until the colour of suspension changes to pale yellow. Then, 10 drops of starch solution are added. The titration continues until the colour of suspension becomes clear white.
(5) It is recommended to repeat the titration (steps 1 through 4) two more times.

Do the following and fill in the answer sheet form

1.5 Write the reactions involved in the procedure of determination of $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ ion.

1.6 Calculate the mass of iron in the solution under analysis, and write your calculations.

problems.title: Qualitative Determination of Paracetamol in a Sample of Unknown Drug
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2. Qualitative Determination of Paracetamol in a Sample of Unknown Drug [printed as Problem 2 (Practical); no points or weight are printed in the source]

Introduction

Three organic compounds are most widely used as pain relieving drugs: acetylsalicylic acid (ortho-acetoxybenzoic acid), phenacetine (para-ethoxyacetanilide), and paracetamol (para-hydroxyacetanilide). Paracetamol is now the most popular, being the base of a large number of well known patented pharmaceuticals (panadol, solpadeine, coldrex, calpol, efferalgan etc.), as it is now considered as the safest and highly efficient drug.

You were given a sample of unknown drug which claims to contain paracetamol. Your task is to prove or disprove this claim experimentally. To do this you shall have to prepare an authentic sample of para-hydroxyacetanilide, and run a thin layer chromatography test.

Reagents

• Para-aminophenol, $3.10\ \mathrm{g}$ in a weighing beaker
• Acetic anhydride, $4.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ in an Erlenmeyer flask
• Ethanol
• Eluent (heptane : ethyl acetate : ethanol = 41 : 47 : 12 by volume)
• Sample of unknown drug in a test tube, 1 % solution in ethanol
• Water (use tap water for all purposes)

Procedure

Preparation of para-hydroxyacetanilide

A $50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ round bottom flask is equipped with reflux condensor and installed on a laboratory stand over a hot plate. Note that the space between the top of hot plate and the bottom of flask be about 1-1.5 cm. Use two clamps to properly support the flask and condenser. Remove the hot plate. Do not switch on the hot plate until you finish with adding reagents and reassembling the apparatus. With reflux condensor temporarily removed, $3.10\ \mathrm{g}$ of para-aminophenol is placed to the flask using a funnel (use a glass rod to push it through the funnel, if necessary). Water ($10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$) is then added through the same funnel. The condenser is mounted back, and acetic anhydride ($4.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$) is carefully poured to the reaction mixture through the condenser (attention! acetic anhydride has a strong irritating smell. In case of spill immediately wash hands with water and ask the supervisor to help with the disposal of spilled compound). Carefully stir the contents by slightly relieving clamps and waving the flask 2 - 3 times. Be careful as the mixture and the flask gets very hot due to the reaction heat. Place back the hot plate and switch it on. The reaction mixture is heated for 15 minutes beginning from the time when you switch on the hot plate. Then, the heater is switched off and removed from the apparatus. The mixture is allowed to cool first by immersing the flask into a bath with cold tap water. You may do this immediately after you remove the plate as the flask is made of highly durable glass. After approximately five minutes unattach the condenser and pour the contents into an empty $100\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ pyrex glass beaker. Put the beaker into a metal dish filled with ice and water. Accurately rub the walls of beaker with spatula and observe the crystallization of crude product as small white crystals.

Assemble a suction filtration device: put the frit filter onto a rubber ring and a heavy-wall flask. Connect the flask to a suction vacuum pump and turn on water in the pump by turning tap. (Attention! Never turn off the water tap if your device is under vacuum. First always disconnect the flask from vacuum pump by carefully pulling off the rubber tubing from the inlet.)

The crystalline precipitate is quantitatively moved onto a filter by spatula. Remaining solid can be washed with small portions of ice cold water (as small as possible, as the compound possesses an essential solubility in water, and the losses of dissolved compound must not outweigh the losses due to incomplete transfer of product to the filter). The product in the filter is carefully washed with 2 - 3 portions of 2 - 3 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of cold water by a) connecting the vacuum suction flask to the atmosphere; b) addition of water and careful mixing it with the precipitate using a spatula; c) reapplying vacuum; d) pressing the precipitate with flat tip of a glass rod to squeeze out as much water as possible.

Several crystals of material are used for chromatography test (see below). All other precipitate is moved to a sheet of filtering paper in a Petri dish, and spread out over the filter in a thin layer, and allowed to dry on a shelf to exclude accidental spill. For rapid drying it is critical to spread it as thin as possible, to break all large pieces, and to stir it and spread again every 3-5 minutes to expose all wet crystals to air. It is established after a numerous repetition of this procedure, that after 30 min the product contains no more than 5 % of water. Such wetness is considered as insignificant for evaluating the results of the preparation.

Chromatography test

(If for some reason you have failed to obtain para-hydroxyacetanilide, you can obtain a sample for chromatography from your supervisor.)

While still wet several crystals of the material obtained by you are dissolved in a tube in 1 - 2 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol. The unknown drug is already dissolved in ethanol and given to you as 1 % solution. These solutions are used for thin layer chromatography, as follows:

Prepare a sheet of chromatography plate covered with silica. Using a sharp pencil draw a start line and marks for sample spots. A small spot of each solution is placed on a chromatography plate using a capillary. The spots are allowed to dry for 1-2 minutes.

The plate is immersed into a beaker containing the eluent and allowed to be eluted. Use forceps to move the plate in and out of the beaker. After the elution, remove the plate from the flask, mark the front of eluent, and allow it to dry under the hood for 5 minutes. Examine the chromatogram under UV light in a special cabinet. Outline the dark spots (if there are any) with a sharp pencil.

Weighting of sample

After you complete the chromatography, your product usually is almost dry and is ready for weighting. Ask you supervisor to weight an empty weighing beaker. Put the dry product into a weighted beaker and give it to the supervisor for weighting. Weights are written in your answer sheet by the supervisor. Calculate the weight of the product.

Do the following and fill in the answer sheet form

2.1 Draw the structures of three main pain relieving drugs mentioned above.

2.2 Draw the reaction equation involved in the preparation of para-hydroxyacetanilide. Calculate the stoichiometric amounts of reagents needed for the reaction. How much acetic anhydride is taken in excess over the stoichiometry? The density of acetic anhydride is $1.08\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

2.3 Calculate the yield of product obtained by you.

2.4 Calculate and compare the values of $R_f$ of unknown drug and your product.

2.5 Is it likely that paracetamol is contained in the sample of drug?

problems.title: Determination of Mg2+ and Ca2+ in Bottled Water
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1. Determination of $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ in Bottled Water [printed as Problem 1 (Practical); no points or weight are printed in the source]

• The $K_{sp}$ for calcium oxalate is $2.3\times10^{-9}$ and the $K_{sp}$ for magnesium oxalate is $8.6\times10^{-5}$.
• In a solution buffered to maintain pH 10, Calmagite indicator is pink when bound to $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ and blue in the absence of available magnesium ions. Calcium ions are not bound by Calmagite.
• EDTA binds to $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ even in the presence of Calmagite. The stoichiometry of the EDTA-metal complex formed with both $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ is 1:1.
• Molar masses: $M(\mathrm{Ca}) = 40.08\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, $M(\mathrm{Mg}) = 24.31\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$

Chemicals Available

• $500\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ sample of “Bottled Water”
• aqueous buffer (pH 10)
• Calmagite indicator
• aqueous saturated ammonium oxalate
• aqueous ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid
• aqueous standardized* $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$
• distilled water

*$0.928\,\mathrm{mg}$ $\ce{Mg^{2+}}/\mathrm{cm^3}$ solution, $0.0382$ moles $\ce{Mg^{2+}}/\mathrm{dm^3}$

Procedure

A. Precipitation of calcium ions

Precipitate the calcium ions in a $25.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of the “Bottled Water” sample by accurately adding approximately $0.50\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of saturated ammonium oxalate solution (from the common burettes in each lab room). Carefully swirl the solution to ensure uniform mixing. Allow at least 45 minutes for complete precipitation to occur.

B. Standardization of the EDTA solution

Using distilled water, dilute $5.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the standardized magnesium solution to a final volume of $100.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$. Add $40\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of distilled water, $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of pH 10 buffer solution, and some Calmagite indicator to $5.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of diluted magnesium solution. Titrate this sample with EDTA solution to a clear blue end point.

Repeat as necessary.

C. Titration of $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$

Add $40\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of distilled water, $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of pH 10 buffer solution, and some Calmagite indicator to $5.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the “Bottled Water” sample. Titrate this sample with EDTA solution to a clear blue end point.

Repeat as necessary.

D. Titration of $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$

Add $40\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of distilled water, $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of pH 10 buffer solution, and some Calmagite indicator to $5.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the calcium-free “Bottled Water” sample prepared in part $\mathbf{A}$. The presence of a small amount of calcium oxalate will not interfere with your titration. Titrate this sample with EDTA solution to a clear blue end point.

Repeat as necessary.

Calculations

Calculate the concentration of $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ (in $\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$) in the “Bottled Water” sample.

Calculate the concentration of $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ (in $\mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}}$) in the “Bottled Water” sample.

problems.title: Organic qualitative analysis
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2. Organic qualitative analysis [printed as Problem 2 (Practical); no points or weight are printed in the source]

You have six bottles containing six different organic compounds. From the list of eight compounds given below, identify the contents of each bottle using the reagents available.

Many of these compounds have strong odours. To prevent the laboratory from becoming too odorous, you must keep each bottle tightly capped when it is not in use. Dispose of any waste produced in the bottle labelled “ORGANIC WASTE” at your station. Also place used litmus paper in this bottle. Keep the waste bottle capped when not in use.

Chemicals Available

• litmus paper, red and blue
• aqueous ceric ammonium nitrate
• aqueous chromic-sulfuric acid
• aqueous 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine
• aqueous 0.2% $\ce{KMnO4}$
• acetone (2-propanone)

Possible Unknowns*

• 2-butanone
• 1-decene
• 2,3-diamino-2,3-dimethylbutane
• hexane
• 3-methyl-1-butanol
• 2-methyl-2-butanol
• nonanal
• propanoic acid

*Several of the unknowns are present as dilute aqueous solutions. This will not interfere with the test results.

problems.title: Synthesis of the Substituted Dihydro-1,3-benzoxazine (C)
problems.problem:
Practical problem 3. Synthesis of the Substituted Dihydro-1,3-benzoxazine (C) [printed as Problem 3 (Practical); no points or weight are printed in the source]

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1997-3-fig1.png

Benzoxazines have long been recognized as useful biologically-active compounds. One such compound ($\mathbf{C}$) will be prepared using the three-step synthesis described below. All of the product obtained in Step I should be used in Step II and similarly all of the product from Step II should be used in Step III. You will be evaluated on both the yield and purity of the final product.

Chemicals available

• $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ reaction vial containing $2.5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanolic 1-amino-4-methylbenzene ($0.22\,\mathrm{g}$),
• vial containing $0.25\,\mathrm{g}$ of 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde,
• vial containing $0.1\,\mathrm{g}$ of sodium borohydride,
• vial containing $0.042\,\mathrm{g}$ of paraformaldehyde,
• test tube containing dilute ethanolic KOH, ($50\,\mathrm{mg}$ of KOH dissolved in $10\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol),
• wash bottle containing dry ethanol,
• Ice is available in each laboratory room.

Molar masses:

$M(\mathrm{H}) = 1.008\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, $M(\mathrm{C}) = 12.011\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, $M(\mathrm{N}) = 14.007\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, $M(\mathrm{O}) = 15.999\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, $M(\mathrm{Na}) = 22.990\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$, $M(\mathrm{B}) = 10.811\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$

Procedure

STEP I

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1997-3-fig2.png

1. Place the small magnetic stirbar in the $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ reaction vial containing solution (i) and stir.
2. Add the 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde from vial (ii) dropwise to the stirred solution in vial (i). After a short period of time a yellow solid will crystallize out. This is intermediate product $\mathbf{A}$.
3. Isolate the yellow solid ($\mathbf{A}$) by vacuum (suction) filtration and wash it with ice-cold ethanol.

STEP II

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1997-3-fig3.png

1. Add the impure Product A from Step I to a $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ reaction vial containing approximately $1.5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol.
2. Surround the vial with ice/water, and stir the reaction vigorously with the spatula while carefully adding small amounts of sodium borohydride (iii) over a period of about 5 minutes until the bright yellow colour disappears. The reaction will bubble. Note that you have been given more sodium borohydride than is required for this reaction.
3. Isolate the intermediate Product B by vacuum (suction) filtration, wash it with ice-cold ethanol, and air dry the solid for approximately 5 minutes.

STEP III

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-1997-3-fig4.png

1. Dissolve all of the paraformaldehyde (iv) in approximately $2.5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanolic potassium hydroxide (v) in a $5\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ vial. Stir to dissolve all of the solid.
2. Add all of product $\mathbf{B}$ from Step II to the vial. Stir and gently reflux the mixture for 15 minutes. A clear solution should be obtained.
3. Concentrate the solution by carefully boiling off some of the ethanol leaving approximately $1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ in the vial and allow the vial to cool. The crystals which form are the required product $\mathbf{C}$.
4. Isolate the crude product $\mathbf{C}$ by vacuum (suction) filtration and air dry the crystals.
5. Recrystallize the crude product from ethanol. Air dry the crystals for 15 minutes.
6. Determine the melting point* and then mass of the final product.
7. Place all of your remaining product in the numbered vial labelled “PRODUCT C” and hand it in for evaluation.

*Note: A melting point is always recorded as a range -- from when the crystals first begin to melt until the last crystal has melted. The melting point apparatus should be allowed to cool to approximately 50 degrees before you use it. The supervisors will be rechecking both your reported melting point and mass for product C.

problems.title: Determination of Calcium by precipitation with oxalate followed by titration with permanganate
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1 (20 points). Determination of Calcium by precipitation with oxalate followed by titration with permanganate [printed as Laboratory Task 1]

In this exercise, you must determine the amount of calcium ion in a solution that contains both calcium and magnesium, by selectively precipitating only the calcium as calcium oxalate, then quantitatively removing the precipitate from the solution by filtration.

$$\ce{Ca^{2+} + C2O4^{2-} <=> CaC2O4 (s)}$$

The precipitate must then be re-dissolved in acid:

$$\ce{CaC2O4 (s) + 2 H+ <=> Ca^{2+} + H2C2O4}$$

and the liberated oxalic acid titrated with standard permanganate solution:

$$\ce{5 H2C2O4 + 2 MnO4^- + 6 H+ <=> 10 CO2 + 2 Mn^{2+} + 8 H2O}$$

Formation of the calcium oxalate precipitate

1. Use a $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ pipette and $250.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ volumetric flask to accurately dilute (by a factor of 10), the calcium/magnesium solution that has been provided for you.

Analyse two samples of the dilute calcium/magnesium solution. You have sufficient reagents for three analyses, but you must plan your time and use of equipment carefully. Take each of your samples through the following procedure:

2. Transfer a $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquot of the dilute calcium/magnesium solution into a $250\,\mathrm{mL}$ beaker, add approximately $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $3\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$ and about $50\,\mathrm{mL}$ of water.

CARE! $3\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$ is very corrosive! The following steps involve hot (nearly boiling) solutions. Be careful and beware of steam!

3. Cover the beaker with a watchglass and gently heat on a hotplate until the solution is very hot, but not boiling.

4. Remove the beaker from the heat, then carefully add solid ammonium oxalate ($1.5\,\mathrm{g}$) and swirl the beaker until most of the ammonium oxalate dissolves.

CARE! Oxalate solutions are toxic. Do not wash solutions that contain oxalate down the sink. Place them in the “Permanganate/Oxalate residues” bottle at the end of your bench.

5. Add 5-10 drops of methyl red indicator to the beaker, then while the solution is hot, increase the pH of the solution by slowly adding 1:1 ammonia solution with constant stirring, until the colour just changes from pink to orange. If you add too much ammonia, the solution will turn yellow. To correct this problem, add 1 drop of $3\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{H2SO4}$ to lower the pH again, then repeat the pH adjustment with ammonia solution.

CARE! 1:1 ammonia solution is corrosive and has a very strong smell! Keep the bottle stoppered when not in use.

6. Allow the solution to stand for at least 60 minutes to quantitatively precipitate the calcium oxalate. Do not stir the solution during this time.

You should complete Laboratory Task 2 during this waiting period.

Do not proceed to the next step until you are confident that precipitation is complete.

Filtration of the calcium oxalate precipitate

7. Prepare a filter paper in a filter funnel supported in the neck of a $250\,\mathrm{mL}$ conical flask. Rinse the paper with a few mL of water then decant most of the supernatant solution from step 6. into the filter funnel. Collect the filtrate in the conical flask. Use a washbottle to rinse the watchglass into the filter funnel.

8. Test the filtrate for the presence of calcium ion by adding a drop of ammonium oxalate test solution to a drop of the filtrate on a black plastic sheet. If a white precipitate (or cloudiness) is formed, the calcium oxalate precipitation in step 6 was unfortunately not complete. Perhaps the pH was not adjusted correctly or insufficient time was allowed for precipitation. Depending on the time you have left, you may start the analysis again or you may continue with the present experiment.

9. If there is no detectable calcium ion in the filtrate, use a washbottle to carefully wash the calcium oxalate precipitate into the filter. Use the rubber “policeman” on the end of a glass rod to remove the last traces of precipitate from the beaker, and rinse these into the filter.

10. Wash the precipitate 4 times with approximately $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ portions of water, collecting the washings in the conical flask.

11. Discard the combined filtrates from the previous steps into the residue bottle labelled “Permanganate/Oxalate residues” then carefully rinse the conical flask with water into the residue bottle.

12. Wash the precipitate one more time with $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ of water. Collect this filtrate in the conical flask and test it for the presence of oxalate by adding a drop of saturated calcium nitrate solution to a drop of the filtrate on a black plastic sheet. If a white precipitate (or cloudiness) is formed, continue washing and testing until the washings are free from oxalate.

13. When the precipitate is free of oxalate, discard the washings and rinse and drain the conical flask.

NOTE! Show your demonstrator your precipitates. You must ask your demonstrator to sign your results sheet before proceeding to the next step.

14. Use a glass rod to break a small hole in the bottom of the filter paper and wash the precipitate through the hole into the conical flask with approximately $20\,\mathrm{mL}$ water. Take care to rinse the rod and the creases of the filter paper.

15. Use a Pasteur pipette to dissolve any traces of calcium oxalate that remain in the paper with $25\,\mathrm{mL}$ $3\,\mathrm{M}$ sulphuric acid, collecting the acid in the conical flask. Finally, rinse the paper with ~ $20\,\mathrm{mL}$ water.

Titration with permanganate

16. Make the volume up to about $100\,\mathrm{mL}$ with water, heat the solution to about 60 °C, then when all the calcium oxalate precipitate is dissolved, carefully titrate the hot solution with standard potassium permanganate solution.

CARE! It is not necessary to measure the temperature of the solution with a thermometer. 60 °C is uncomfortably hot to touch.

17. Discard the titrated solution into the residue bottle labelled “Permanganate/Oxalate residues”.

Calculate the average concentration of calcium ion in the original calcium/magnesium solution that was provided.

Atomic masses: Ca 40.08, Mg 24.31, Mn 54.94, C 12.01, O 16.00 g/mol

[Results sheet, printed “Laboratory Task 1 Results Sheet” (printed “20 marks”); blank template reconstructed from the printed headings:]

Analysis of calcium/magnesium solution

Ca/Mg solution: Blue Red Green Orange (circle one)

Permanganate titration

Concentration of standard $\ce{KMnO4}$: ____ M

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|l} \text{titration number:} & 1 & 2 & 3 & \\ \hline \text{initial burette reading} & & & & \mathrm{mL} \\ \text{final burette reading} & & & & \mathrm{mL} \\ \text{volume of standard }\ce{KMnO4} & & & & \mathrm{mL} \end{array}$$

Average concentration of $\ce{Ca^{2+}}$ in Ca/Mg solution: ____ M

problems.title: Analysis of a mixture of cobalt(III) complexes
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2 (20 points). Analysis of a mixture of cobalt(III) complexes [printed as Laboratory Task 2]

When the complex $\ce{[Co(NH3)5NO2]Cl2}$ is prepared in the laboratory, it often contains a considerable amount of $\ce{[Co(NH3)6]Cl3}$ byproduct.

In this exercise, you must determine the amount of $\ce{[Co(NH3)5NO2]Cl2}$ in a sample that also contains only $\ce{[Co(NH3)6]Cl3}$ as a byproduct, using a cation-exchange procedure.

The cation exchange resin used in this exercise is a cross-linked polystyrene resin of the strong acid type. It contains $-\ce{SO3H}$ groups from which the $\ce{H+}$ can be exchanged.

When a solution containing 1 mol of $\ce{M^{n+}}$ is allowed to react with the resin this liberates $n$ mol of $\ce{H+}$. In this exercise, the solution resulting from ion exchange of the mixture of the two different complex cations is used to titrate a standardised NaOH solution.

Preparation of the cation exchange resin

You are provided with about $10\,\mathrm{g}$ of wet resin in the $\ce{H+}$ form. Wash the resin using the following procedure to remove all traces of free acid:

1. Transfer your resin to a $250\,\mathrm{mL}$ beaker, washing it from the container with about $50\,\mathrm{mL}$ of water, then let the resin settle. This will take a few minutes.

2. Carefully pour off (decant) as much of the acidic solution as possible into a ‘waste’ beaker. Try to minimise loss of any of the resin in this process. Wash the resin with ~$20\,\mathrm{mL}$ portions of distilled water and test a drop of washing solution using a glass rod and pH paper until the excess acid is completely removed (pH ~5). You should not need to use more than $200\,\mathrm{mL}$ of water to do this.

3. Drain off all but enough water to leave the resin just covered with water.

Be sure to put all your acidic wash solutions into a waste bottle labelled “acid waste” - not down the sink! Do not allow the resin to dry out.

Preparation and standardisation of approximately $0.0125\,\mathrm{M}$ NaOH

4. Prepare $250.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ of approximately $0.0125\,\mathrm{M}$ NaOH by accurately diluting your ~$0.125\,\mathrm{M}$ NaOH with distilled water in a volumetric flask.

5. With the standard $0.01253\,\mathrm{M}$ HCl that is provided, titrate $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquots of the diluted NaOH solution, using phenolphthalein indicator.

Analysis Procedure

You are provided with approximately $40\,\mathrm{mL}$ of a $0.005000\,\mathrm{M}$ solution of HCl that contains $0.2000\,\mathrm{g}$ of a mixture of the cobalt(III) complexes $\ce{[Co(NH3)5NO2]Cl2}$ and $\ce{[Co(NH3)6]Cl3}$ in $40.00\,\mathrm{mL}$.

6. Use a pipette to transfer a $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquot of the cobalt complex solution into a $250\,\mathrm{mL}$ beaker (beaker #1) and add ~$25\,\mathrm{mL}$ water.

7. Use a plastic spoon to add about half (~$5\,\mathrm{g}$) of your wet resin to the cobalt(III) solution and allow to stand for at least 5 minutes for ion- exchange to take place, liberating $\ce{H+}$. You should occasionally gently swirl the mixture to hasten the ion-exchange process.

8. Carefully wash the acidic solution into a second $250\,\mathrm{mL}$ beaker (beaker #2) with about $20\,\mathrm{mL}$ of distilled water. Try to leave as much as possible of the resin behind.

Notice that the solution is now much lighter in color, indicating that most, but not all of the cobalt complex mixture is stuck to the resin. You must now remove the last traces of cobalt(III) from solution (liberating more acid in the process), with a second batch of resin.

9. Add most of the remainder of your resin (~$4\,\mathrm{g}$) to the solution in beaker #2 and again allow to stand for at least 5 minutes to allow the cation exchange to take place, liberating more $\ce{H+}$.

At the end of this process, the solution should be colorless - if not, (perhaps you did not wait long enough for ion-exchange to take place) repeat the ion-exchange and washing steps with the last portion (~$1\,\mathrm{g}$) of your ion-exchange resin.

10. Filter the two resin samples through a carefully washed filter paper, and collect the acidic filtrate in a $100\,\mathrm{mL}$ volumetric flask. Carefully wash the resin with small portions of water into the volumetric flask and make up to the mark with water.

11. With this acid solution, titrate $25.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquots of your standardised NaOH solution.

Calculate the number of moles of $\ce{H+}$ liberated by the $25\,\mathrm{mL}$ aliquot of your mixture of cobalt(III) complexes and report the percentage of $\ce{[Co(NH3)5NO2]Cl2}$ that is present in your sample.

problems.title: A Kinetic Study of the Acid Catalysed Reaction Between Acetone and Iodine in Aqueous Solution
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1 (50 points). A Kinetic Study of the Acid Catalysed Reaction Between Acetone and Iodine in Aqueous Solution [printed as Laboratory Task I]

Do not start Laboratory Task 2 until you have finished Laboratory Task 1. The experimental part of Laboratory Task 1 can be completed in approximately 1.5 hours (calculation time not included).

INTRODUCTION

The reaction between acetone and iodine in aqueous solution is catalyzed by $\ce{H+}$.

$$\ce{CH3-CO-CH3 (aq) + I2 (aq) ->[H+] CH3-CO-CH2I (aq) + H+ (aq) + I- (aq)}$$

In this experiment, the kinetics of the iodination is measured to determine the rate law of the reaction. The rate equation for the loss of $\ce{I2}$(aq) has been shown to have the form

$$\text{Rate} = -\frac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{I2}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k[\ce{CH3COCH3}]^{x}[\ce{I2}]^{y}[\ce{H+}]^{z}$$

where $\ce{H+}$ ions are the catalyst.

In order to determine the rate constant k and the kinetic orders x, y and z, the initial rate of reaction is measured.

$$\text{Initial rate} = k[\ce{CH3COCH3}]_0^{x}[\ce{I2}]_0^{y}[\ce{H+}]_0^{z}$$

Where $[\ ]_0$ are the initial concentrations of acetone, $\ce{I2}$ and $\ce{H+}$, respectively.

If the initial rates are measured for various initial concentrations of the reactants then the order with respect to each reactant can be obtained.

The initial rate is obtained by measuring the decrease in the $\ce{I2}$(aq) concentration after a short time interval (7.0 min. in this experiment) after the start of the reaction. Aqueous sodium acetate solution is added to stop the reaction after 7 minutes. The acetate ion reacts immediately with the $\ce{H+}$ to produce acetic acid and so reducing the concentration of $\ce{H+}$. The reaction is thus stopped as there is no catalyst present.

Since the reaction does not come to a complete halt, the solution should be titrated immediately after the addition of the sodium acetate solution.

The remaining iodine $\ce{I2}$ (aq) is determined by titration with sodium thiosulphate, $\ce{Na2S2O3}$. As the end point of the titration is approached, starch indicator is added and the titration is continued until the blue colour disappears.

Equipments

$$\begin{array}{r|l|c} 1. & \text{Glass stoppered flask }250\,\mathrm{mL} & 5 \\ 2. & \text{Erlenmeyer flask }125\,\mathrm{mL} & 3 \\ 3. & \text{Burette }25\,\mathrm{mL} & 1 \\ 4. & \text{Pipette }5\,\mathrm{mL} & 4 \\ 5. & \text{Pipette }10\,\mathrm{mL} & 3 \\ 6. & \text{Pipette filler bulb with tip} & 1 \\ 7. & \text{Beaker }100\,\mathrm{mL} & 1 \\ 8. & \text{Beaker }50\,\mathrm{mL} & 3 \\ 9. & \text{Beaker }250\,\mathrm{mL}\text{ (labeled waste disposal)} & 1 \\ 10. & \text{Graduated cylinder }10\,\mathrm{mL} & 1 \\ 11. & \text{Wash bottle }500\,\mathrm{mL} & 1 \\ 12. & \text{Stop-watch} & 1 \\ 13. & \text{Pen} & 1 \\ 14. & \text{Label sheet} & 1 \end{array}$$

Chemicals

$$\begin{array}{r|l|l} 1. & \text{Aqueous iodine solution in }0.4\,\mathrm{M}\ \ce{KI} & 80\,\mathrm{mL} \\ 2. & 0.100\,\mathrm{M}\text{ aq. }\ce{HCl} & 50\,\mathrm{mL} \\ 3. & 0.50\,\mathrm{M}\text{ aq. }\ce{CH3COONa} & 80\,\mathrm{mL} \\ 4. & \text{Standard }0.02\text{xxx}\,\mathrm{M}\ \ce{Na2S2O3}\text{(aq) solution} & 200\,\mathrm{mL} \\ & \text{(the exact concentration will be announced at the beginning of Task 1)} & \\ 5. & \text{Aqueous acetone (50\% by volume)} & 50\,\mathrm{mL} \\ & \text{(density of pure acetone; }0.787\,\mathrm{g/mL},\ \text{MW} = 58.08\text{)} & \\ 6. & \text{Starch indicator} & 7\,\mathrm{mL} \end{array}$$

Stop-watch Operation

A = Mode button (right bottom)

B = Start/Stop button (right top)

C = Split/Reset button (left top)

Mode is already set. Do not touch the button A.

1. Check that the display is $0.00_{00}$. If not, call demonstrator.
2. To start, press B.
3. To stop, press B.
4. To reset, press C.

Procedure

A. Standardisation of Iodine Solution

1. Pipet $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of aqueous iodine into a clean $125\,\mathrm{mL}$ Erlenmeyer flask.
2. Add $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ of distilled water using graduated cylinder.
3. Titrate the iodine with the standard $0.02\text{xxx}\,\mathrm{M}$ sodium thiosulfate solution until the colour of the solution is pale yellow.
4. Add 3 - 4 drops of starch indicator and continue the titration until the blue colour disappears.
5. Record the initial and the final volumes of the thiosulfate solution and the volume used in the answer sheet.
6. Repeat the titration as necessary (Steps 1 to 5)
7. Give the titre volume for calculation in the answer sheet.
8. Calculate the iodine concentration.

B. A kinetic study of acid catalysed reaction between acetone and iodine in aqueous solution

1. Label the stoppered flasks as follows: Flask I, II, III and IV.
2. To each respective flask add the following volumes of distilled water, $0.100\,\mathrm{M}$ hydrochloric acid and 50% acetone: Stopper each flask immediately after addition of the solutions.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} & \text{Volume (mL)} & &  \\ \text{Flask No.} & \text{water} & 0.100\,\mathrm{M}\ \ce{HCl} & \text{50\%acetone} \\ \hline \text{I} & 5.00 & 5.00 & 5.00 \\ \text{II} & 0.0 & 5.00 & 5.00 \\ \text{III} & 0.0 & 5.00 & 10.00 \\ \text{IV} & 0.0 & 10.00 & 5.00 \end{array}$$

3. Measure out $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ of $0.50\,\mathrm{M}$ aq. $\ce{CH3COONa}$ into the graduated cylinder.
4. Set the stop-watch to $0.00_{00}$ display.
5. Pipette $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ of iodine solution into the stoppered Flask No. I. Start the stop-watch as soon as the first drop of iodine solution is added.
6. Stopper the flask and swirl continuously.
7. Just before 7.0 min, remove the stopper, at 7.0 min, immediately pour $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ of sodium acetate solution (from step 3) into the reaction flask. Shake well.
8. Titrate the remaining iodine with standard thiosulphate solution.
9. Record the volume of the thiosulphate solution.
10. Repeat the above steps (Steps 3 to 9) for Flask II, III and IV but add in step 5 the $\ce{I2}$(aq) solution to each flask as indicated:

• Flask II: $10.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ $\ce{I2}$ solution
• Flask III: $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ $\ce{I2}$ solution
• Flask IV: $5.00\,\mathrm{mL}$ $\ce{I2}$ solution

Calculations

B-1. Calculate the initial concentrations (M) of iodine, acetone and HCl solutions in Flasks I to IV, assuming volumes are additive.

B-2. Calculate concentrations of iodine (M) remaining in Flasks I to IV at 7.0 minutes.

B-3. Calculate the initial reaction rate for Flasks I to IV in $\mathrm{M\,s^{-1}}$.

B-4. The rate of reaction has the form

$$\text{Rate} = -\frac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{I2}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = k[\ce{CH3COCH3}]^{x}[\ce{I2}]^{y}[\ce{H+}]^{z}$$

Calculate the reaction orders x, y and z from the initial rates and the initial concentrations of acetone, iodine and HCl. The values of x, y and z should be rounded off to the nearest integer and fill in the answer sheet. Write rate equation or rate law.

B-5. Calculate the rate constant, k, for Flasks I to IV with proper unit.

B-6. Give the mean value of the rate constant.

problems.title: Isolation and Identification of an Essential Oil from Natural Source
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2 (28.6 points). Isolation and Identification of an Essential Oil from Natural Source [printed as Laboratory Task II]

In this experiment, you will steam distil and determine the structures of the main essential oil ($\mathbf{S}$) from a given natural source and a product from its chemical conversion (unknown $\mathbf{Y}$).

To determine the structures, you have to use organic qualitative analysis to identify any functional groups present in the compounds by using the reagents at your station. NMR data will be given only after the functional group test is completed.

Chemicals Available:

• Sample (1 g in a vial)
• Unknown $\mathbf{Y}$ (in a vial)
• Anhydrous $\ce{Na2SO4}$ (in a plastic vial)
• Dichloromethane
• Ceric ammonium nitrate solution
• 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine (labelled as 2,4-DNP)
• 2% aq. $\ce{NH3}$
• 5% aq. $\ce{AgNO3}$
• 5% aq. HCl
• 5% aq. NaOH
• 5% aq. $\ce{NaHCO3}$
• 1% $\ce{FeCl3}$ in EtOH
• 0.2% aq. $\ce{KMnO4}$: Decolourised with easily oxidised functional groups.
• Acetone (for washing)

Equipment's and Glassware's

$$\begin{array}{r|l|l} 1. & \text{Microscale kit} & \text{1 set} \\ 2. & \text{Round bottomed flask, }25\,\mathrm{mL} & 1 \\ 3. & \text{Hotplate-stirrer/stand/clamps} & \text{1 set} \\ 4. & \text{Sand bath} & 1 \\ 5. & \text{Beaker }(250\,\mathrm{mL}) & 1 \\ 6. & \text{Test tube} & 16 \\ 7. & \text{Test tube rack} & 1 \\ 8. & \text{Pasteur pipette} & 8 \\ 9. & \text{Rubber bulb} & 1 \\ 10. & \text{Microspatula} & 1 \\ 11. & \text{Rubber tubing (1 m)} & 2 \\ 12. & \text{Thermometer} & 2 \\ 13. & \text{Wooden ring} & 2 \\ 14. & \text{A bag of tissue paper} & 1 \\ 15. & \text{A bag of cotton/a piece of paper} & \text{1 set} \\ 16. & \text{Cotton gloves} & \text{1 pair} \\ 17. & \text{Vial (for recovered dichloromethane)} & 1 \\ 18. & \text{Wooden stick} & 1 \\ 19. & \text{Ice (in a bucket in each lab)} & \end{array}$$

Procedure:

Apparatus. Assemble a distillation apparatus (as shown in the diagram 1) using a $25\,\mathrm{mL}$ round bottomed flask for distillation and a $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ round bottomed flask to collect the distillate. Heat the sand bath to approximately $150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ before proceeding the next step.

Simplified Steam Distillation: Mix 1 g of ground sample with $15\,\mathrm{mL}$ of water in the $25\,\mathrm{mL}$ round bottomed flask and allow the sample to soak in the water for about 10 minutes before distillation. Do not forget to put in a magnetic bar, turn on the water in the condenser and stirring motor, heat the mixture (the temperature of the sand bath should not be below $170\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) to provide a steady rate of distillation. At least $5\,\mathrm{mL}$ of distillate must be collected. Hot plate must be turned off after distillation is finished. Disassemble the apparatus and rinse the condenser with acetone. Be sure that the condenser is dry before using in the next step

Q.1) (0 or 5 marks) Show the distillate to your demonstrator and ask for his or her signature on your answer sheet before proceeding to the next step.

Extraction of the Essential Oil: Transfer the distillate to a $15\,\mathrm{mL}$ capped centrifuge tube and add $1\,\mathrm{mL}$ of dichloromethane to extract the distillate. Cap the tube securely and shake vigorously, cool in ice. Allow the layers to separate.

Using a Pasteur pipette, transfer the dichloromethane layer to a $10\,\mathrm{mL}$ test tube. Repeat this extraction with fresh $1\,\mathrm{mL}$ dichloromethane twice and combine with the first extract.

Drying: Dry the dichloromethane extract by adding anhydrous $\ce{Na2SO4}$ and stir occasionally for 10 minutes.

Evaporation: With a clean, dry cotton plugged Pasteur pipette transfer the organic layer to a dry $5\,\mathrm{mL}$ conical vial. Use approximately $1\,\mathrm{mL}$ of clean dichloromethane to wash $\ce{Na2SO4}$ using the dry cotton plugged Pasteur pipette, then transfer into the vial. Be careful not to transfer any of the $\ce{Na2SO4}$ into the vial. Use Hickman still head and dry condenser (see diagram 2) to distil the dichloromethane from the solution until the volume is reduced to $1\,\mathrm{mL}$. Discard the distilled dichloromethane from the Hickman still head with a Pasteur pipette or a syringe to a vial (for recovered dichloromethane) and keep the residue for functional group analysis.

Functional Group Analysis: Carry out the functional group analysis of the residue solution ($1\,\mathrm{mL}$) by using the appropriate reagents at your station. (Note: dichloromethane is immiscible with water.)

Tollen's Reagent: add 1 drop of 5% aq. $\ce{AgNO3}$ in a small test tube followed by 1 drop of 5% aq. NaOH, brown precipitate will appear. Add 2% aq $\ce{NH3}$ to the tube until all the precipitate dissolved. The solution is ready for the test.

Q.2) (5.5) Fill in your results in the answer sheet and indicate the functional group(s) present or not present.

Structure elucidation of the main essential oil ($\mathbf{S}$): Reaction of the main essential oil ($\mathbf{S}$) with $\ce{CH3I}$ in the presence of $\ce{K2CO3}$ gives compound $\mathbf{X}$ ($\ce{C11H14O2}$). Oxidation of $\mathbf{X}$ gives unknown $\mathbf{Y}$ ($\ce{C10H12O4}$) as the main product and $\ce{CO2}$.

Q.3) (7) Identify the functional groups of unknown $\mathbf{Y}$ (provided in a conical vial) by using the reagents at your station and fill in your results in the answer sheet. Indicate the functional group(s) present or not present.

Hand in your copy of answer sheet PART I (Demonstrator copy) of functional group analysis with your signature and ask for $^{1}\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectra and answer sheet PART II. $^{1}\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectra will be given only when the functional group analysis is completed.

Q.4) (6) Draw the structure which represents the main component in the essential oil (S) that was distilled from the sample. Assign each proton from the provided $^{1}\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectra by labelling the peak number on the proton in the structure in the answer sheet.

Q.5) (5) Draw the structures of compound X and unknown Y. Assign each proton of unknown Y from the provided $^{1}\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectra in the same manner as Q.4.
