You have 10 different compounds dissolved in water in 5 unknown solutions. Each numbered container contains two of the following compounds in aqueous solution (every compound is used, and each compound is used only once):

$\ce{AgNO3}$, $\ce{Al2(SO4)3}$, $\ce{Ba(NO3)2}$, $\ce{Fe(NO3)3}$, $\ce{KI}$, $\ce{KIO3}$, $\ce{Na2CO3}$, $\ce{Na2SO3}$, $\ce{MgCl2}$, $\ce{NH3}$

You are given $\ce{HNO3}$ solution, NaOH solution, hexane and the aqueous solutions of the 10 pure compounds listed above.

You can use empty test tubes and any of the liquids provided (including the unknowns) to identify the unknown samples. A funnel and filter paper can be used for separation.

Identify the compounds in the solutions 1-5. Give the number of the solution that contains the individual compounds on the answer sheet. Indicate two observations caused by a chemical reaction for each compound in your unknown mixtures by giving the letter code of the appropriate observation (choose one or more from the list), and write appropriate balanced ionic equation(s) that explain the observation. At least one of the reactions has to be specific for clearly identifying the compound from this selection of unknowns.

Note: After the STOP signal close all the centrifuge test tubes containing the unknown mixtures with the blue caps labeled with the student code and leave these in the rack.

[Answer sheet, 7 points for each of the 10 compounds, total 70:] Only fill out this table when you are ready with all your assignments. Use the following observation codes:

• B - Formation of colored precipitate (red, brown, yellow, black etc.)
• C - Dissolution of precipitate
• D - Color change in the solution
• E - Formation of colored solution
• F - Brown color in the organic phase
• G - Purple color in the organic phase
• H - Formation of colored gas
• I - Formation of colorless and odorless gas
• J - Formation of colorless and odorous gas
• K – Change in the color of precipitate

problems.title: Determination of fluoride and chloride content in mineral water
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2 (95 points / 14% of the total). Determination of fluoride and chloride content in mineral water [printed as Task 2]

Labware (Task 2)

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \textbf{Item} & \textbf{Quantity} \\ \hline \textbf{Tasks 2 and 3, for each student, on the table} & \\ \text{Container with a screw cap for waste, 3 dm}^3\text{, labeled “Liquid Waste, Tests 2\&3”} & 1 \\ \hline \textbf{Task 2, for each student, on the table} & \\ \text{Storage box labeled “Task 2”} & 1 \\ \text{Laboratory stand with double burette clamp} & 1 \\ \text{Burette, 25.00 cm}^3 & 2 \\ \text{Graduated pipette, 10.0 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Graduated pipette, 1.00 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Bulb (Mohr) pipette, 10.00 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Erlenmeyer flask, 100 cm}^3 & 2 \\ \text{Graduated cylinder, 10.0 cm}^3 & 2 \\ \text{Brush} & 1 \\ \text{Polypropylene funnel, 5.5 cm} & 1 \\ \hline \textbf{Task 2, for each student, in the storage box “Task 2”} & \\ \text{Polystyrene test tubes, 10 cm}^3 & 8 \\ \text{Pipette filler} & 1 \\ \text{Pasteur pipettes for indicators} & 2 \end{array}$$

Chemicals (Task 2)

$$\begin{array}{l|l|c|c|l|l} \textbf{Name} & \textbf{State} & \textbf{Conc.} & \textbf{Q-ty} & \textbf{Placed in} & \textbf{Labeled} \\ \hline \textbf{Task 2, for each student, on the table} & & & & & \\ \text{Nitric acid} & \text{Aqueous solution} & 2\ \mathrm{M} & -\text{*} & \text{Glass bottle with dropper cap, 250 cm}^3 & \ce{HNO3} \\ \hline \textbf{Task 2, for each student, in the storage box “Task 2”} & & & & & \\ \text{Water sample solution} & \text{Aqueous solution} & \text{To be determined} & 100\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Glass bottle with screw cap, 100 cm}^3 & \text{Water sample} \\ \text{Sodium fluoride} & \text{Aqueous solution} & 9\ \mathrm{mg/dm^3}\text{ in fluoride} & 50\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Glass bottle with screw cap, 50 cm}^3 & \ce{F-}\text{, 9 mg/dm}^3 \\ \text{Zirconyl Alizarin indicator} & \text{Acidic aqueous solutions} & 0.055\%\ \ce{ZrOCl2}\text{, 0.028\% Alizarin Red S} & 10\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Glass bottle with screw cap, 25 cm}^3 & \text{Zirconyl Alizarin} \\ \text{Sodium chloride} & \text{Aqueous solution} & 0.0500\ \mathrm{M} & 50\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Glass bottle with screw cap, 50 cm}^3 & \text{NaCl, 0.0500 M} \\ \text{Ammonium iron(III) sulfate dodecahydrate} & \text{Aqueous acidic solution} & 20\ \mathrm{g/dm^3} & 10\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Glass bottle, 15 cm}^3 & \ce{Fe^{3+}}\text{ ind.} \\ \text{Silver nitrate} & \text{Aqueous solution} & \text{To be determined} & 200\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Amber glass bottle, 250 cm}^3 & \ce{AgNO3} \\ \text{Ammonium thiocyanate} & \text{Aqueous solution} & \text{See exact concentration on the label} & 100\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Glass bottle with screw cap, 100 cm}^3 & \ce{NH4SCN}\text{, X.XXXX M} \\ \text{Potassium chromate} & \text{Aqueous solution} & 10\% & 5\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Glass bottle, 15 cm}^3 & \ce{K2CrO4} \end{array}$$

(*) In the quantity left after doing Task 1.

Georgia is world famous for its splendid mineral waters. Many of these are used to cure various diseases. Manufacturers have to carefully control the ionic composition of waters, fluoride and chloride being among the most important ions.

Visual colorimetric detection of fluoride

The method of fluoride determination is based on the decrease in the color intensity of zirconium(IV)-Alizarin Red S complex in the presence of fluoride ions due to formation of a more stable colorless complex. The equilibrium is achieved in about 20 minutes after the reagent addition. The fluoride concentration is determined visually by comparing the color developed in the sample with those in the calibration solutions.

Transfer $9.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of mineral water from the sample into the plastic test tube labeled “X”.

Calculate how much of the $9.0\ \mathrm{mg/dm^3}$ standard fluoride solution you will need to prepare a set of calibration solutions with the following fluoride ion content: 0.0; 1.0; 2.0; 3.5; 5.0; 6.5; $8.0\ \mathrm{mg/dm^3}$ (calculate for $9.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of each solution).

Using the $1.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ and $10.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ graduated pipettes, add the calculated amounts of the standard fluoride solution to the test-tubes, then add $1.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of Zirconyl Alizarin indicator into each test tube, and bring the volume in each calibration test tube to the $10.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ mark with distilled water (the mark is shown in the figure with the arrow).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2016-2-fig1.png

2.1.1. (2 pt) Report the fluoride volumes used in your dilutions.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \ce{F-}\text{ content (mg/dm}^3\text{)} & 0.0 & 1.0 & 2.0 & 3.5 & 5.0 & 6.5 & 8.0 \\ \hline \text{Calculated volume of }\ce{F-}\text{ solution (cm}^3\text{)} & & & & & & & \end{array}$$

Mix the obtained solutions in the test tubes. Set the tube rack aside for at least 20 minutes.

2.1.2. (15 pt) Compare the color of the sample and the calibration solutions looking on them from the top down and from the front. Select the concentration of the standard that is closest to the fluoride concentration of the water sample.

[Answer sheet: Circle the concentration of the standard that is closest to the fluoride concentration of the water sample.]

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} \ce{F-}\text{ content (mg/dm}^3\text{)} & 0.0 & 1.0 & 2.0 & 3.5 & 5.0 & 6.5 & 8.0 \end{array}$$

Note: the rack with the test tubes will be photographed by the lab staff after the whole exam is finished.

Standardization of silver nitrate solution by the Mohr method

Transfer $10.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the standard $0.0500\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ NaCl solution into an Erlenmeyer flask using the bulb (Mohr) pipette. Add approximately $20\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of distilled water and 10 drops of 10% aqueous $\ce{K2CrO4}$ solution.

Fill a burette with the silver nitrate solution. Titrate the contents of the flask with the silver nitrate solution while vigorously mixing the solution containing the precipitate formed. The final titrant drops are added slowly with vigorous swirling of the flask. The titration is complete when the faint color change visible on titrant addition does not disappear in the pure yellow suspension. Take the final burette reading. Repeat the titration as necessary.

2.2.1. (30 pt) Report your volumes on the answer sheet.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Titration no.} & 1 & 2 & & & & \\ \hline \text{Initial burette reading, cm}^3 & & & & & & \\ \text{Final burette reading, cm}^3 & & & & & & \\ \text{Volume spent, cm}^3 & & & & & & \end{array}$$

Your accepted volume, $V_1$: …… $\mathrm{cm^3}$

2.2.2. (2 pt) Write balanced chemical equations for the titration of NaCl with $\ce{AgNO3}$ and for the end-point indication reaction.

2.2.3. (2 pt) Calculate the concentration of the $\ce{AgNO3}$ solution from your measurement.

2.2.4. (2 pt) The Mohr titration method requires a neutral medium. Write down equations for the interfering reactions that take place at lower and at higher pH.

Chloride determination by the Volhard method

Wash the bulb (Mohr) pipette with distilled water. Wash the Erlenmeyer flasks first with a small portion of the ammonia solution left over from Task 1 to help removing the silver salt precipitate and then with distilled water. (In case you used up all the ammonia solution in the first task, you can get a refill without penalty.)

Transfer a $10.0\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ aliquot of the mineral water from the sample into an Erlenmeyer flask using the bulb (Mohr) pipette. Add $5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $2\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ nitric acid using a graduated cylinder. Add $20.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the silver nitrate solution from the burette and mix well the suspension. Add appr. $2\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the indicator ($\ce{Fe^{3+}}$) solution with the Pasteur pipette.

Fill the second burette with the standard ammonium thiocyanate solution (see the exact concentration on the label). Titrate the suspension with this solution while vigorously swirling. At the end point one drop produces a faint brown color that is stable even after intense mixing. Take the final burette reading. Repeat the titration as necessary.

Note. The AgCl precipitate exchanges $\ce{Cl-}$ ions with $\ce{SCN-}$ ions from the solution. If you titrate too slowly or with breaks, the brown color disappears with time, and too much titrant is spent for the titration. Therefore when approaching the endpoint you should add the titrant at a constant slow rate swirling the flask constantly so that the suspension would stay white. The appearance of faint brown color will mean reaching the endpoint.

2.3.1. (30 pt) Report your volumes on the answer sheet.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c|c|c} \text{Titration no.} & 1 & 2 & & & & \\ \hline \text{Initial burette reading, cm}^3 & & & & & & \\ \text{Final burette reading, cm}^3 & & & & & & \\ \text{Volume spent, cm}^3 & & & & & & \end{array}$$

Your accepted volume, $V_2$: …… $\mathrm{cm^3}$

2.3.2. (2 pt) Write down balanced chemical equations for the back titration with $\ce{NH4SCN}$ and that for the end-point indication reaction.

2.3.3. (4 pt) Calculate the chloride concentration (in $\mathrm{mg/dm^3}$) in the water sample from your measurements.

2.3.4. (2 pt) If $\ce{Br-}$, $\ce{I-}$, and $\ce{F-}$ ions are present in the sample in addition to chloride, the concentration of which ion(s) will contribute to the result of the Volhard titration? [Answer sheet: Tick the appropriate box(es).]

□ $\ce{Br-}$ □ $\ce{I-}$ □ $\ce{F-}$ □ none

2.3.5. (4 pt) When trying to determine the concentration of $\ce{Cl-}$ in the presence of other halides, an analyst added some potassium iodate and sulfuric acid to the sample and boiled the solution. Afterwards he reduced the excess of iodate to iodine by boiling the sample with phosphorous acid $\ce{H3PO3}$. What interfering anions were removed by this operation? Write the chemical equations for the reactions of these ions with iodate.

[Answer sheet options for the interfering anions:] □ $\ce{Br-}$ □ $\ce{I-}$ □ $\ce{F-}$ □ none

problems.title: Identifying flavors and fragrances
problems.problem:
Practical problem 3 (60 points / 13% of the total). Identifying flavors and fragrances [printed as Task 3]

Labware (Task 3)

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \textbf{Item} & \textbf{Quantity} \\ \hline \textbf{Task 3, for each student, get from the lab assistants} & \\ \text{Storage box labeled “Task 3”} & 1 \\ \hline \textbf{Task 3, for each student, in the storage box “Task 3”} & \\ \text{Polystyrene test tubes, 10 cm}^3 & 20 \\ \text{Alcohol lamp} & 1 \\ \text{Test tube holders, wooden} & 1 \\ \text{Glass test tubes} & 10 \\ \text{Pasteur pipettes} & 10 \\ \text{Strong plastic cup} & 1 \end{array}$$

Chemicals (Task 3)

$$\begin{array}{l|l|c|c|l|l} \textbf{Name} & \textbf{State} & \textbf{Conc.} & \textbf{Q-ty} & \textbf{Placed in} & \textbf{Labeled} \\ \hline \textbf{Task 3, for each student, on the table} & & & & & \\ \text{Ethanol} & \text{Liquid} & 95\ \% & 150\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Glass bottle with dropper cup, 250 cm}^3 & \ce{C2H5OH} \\ \hline \textbf{Task 3, for each student, in the storage box “Task 3”} & & & & & \\ \text{Organic unknowns 1 to 8} & \text{Liquid} & - & 0.5\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Syringes, 2 cm}^3 & \text{1 to 8} \\ \text{Potassium permanganate} & \text{Aqueous solution} & 0.13\ \% & 5\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Amber glass bottle, 50 cm}^3 & \ce{KMnO4} \\ \text{Ammonium cerium(IV) nitrate reagent} & \text{2.0 M HNO}_3\text{ aqueous solution} & 28.6\ \% & 5\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{HDPE bottle, 30 cm}^3 & \text{Ce(IV)} \\ \text{Acetonitrile} & \text{Liquid} & - & 45\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{Glass bottle, 50 cm}^3 & \ce{CH3CN} \\ \text{2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine reagent} & \text{Sulfuric acid solution in aqueous ethanol} & 3\ \% & 20\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{HDPE bottle, 30 cm}^3 & \text{DNPH} \\ \text{Iron(III) chloride} & \text{0.5 M HCl aqueous solution} & 2.5\ \% & 1\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{HDPE bottle, 30 cm}^3 & \ce{FeCl3} \\ \text{Hydroxylamine hydrochloride} & \text{Ethanolic solution} & 0.5\ \mathrm{M} & 10\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{HDPE bottle, 30 cm}^3 & \ce{NH2OH}\times\text{HCl} \\ \text{Sodium hydroxide} & \text{Aqueous solution} & 6\ \mathrm{M} & 5\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{HDPE bottle, 30 cm}^3 & \ce{NaOH} \\ \text{Hydrochloric acid} & \text{Aqueous solution} & 1\ \mathrm{M} & 25\ \mathrm{cm^3} & \text{HDPE bottle, 30 cm}^3 & \ce{HCl} \end{array}$$

Tourists coming to Georgia admire many specialties, local cuisine occupying one of the top positions in the list of adventures. Excellent meat, fresh vegetables and greens, ripe fruits, home-made jams… What else is needed to satisfy true gourmets? Of course, unique flavors and fragrances!

You are given 8 samples of unknown organic compounds (labeled 1 to 8), which are industrially used as flavors and fragrances. All samples are pure individual compounds. Their possible structures are found among $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{M}$ given here.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2016-3-fig1.png

The organic compounds in your unknown samples are readily soluble in ether, and insoluble in dilute aqueous NaOH and HCl. These compounds, but the unknown No. 6. are insoluble in water, the latter being slightly soluble ($3.5\ \mathrm{g/dm^3}$).

3.1. (32 pt) Perform test reactions described below to identify the samples 1-8. Indicate the results of the tests by giving the Roman numeral of the appropriate observation (choose one or more from the list). Fill in all cells of the table. Use + and – to indicate positive and negative tests.

Test procedures

$\ce{KMnO4}$ test (Baeyer test)

Place appr. $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of 95% ethanol in a plastic test tube and add 1 drop of an unknown. Add 1 drop of $\ce{KMnO4}$ solution and shake the mixture. Treat the test as positive if the permanganate color disappears immediately after shaking.

3.3. (4 pt) Write the reaction scheme for a positive Baeyer test with one of the compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{M}$.

Cerium(IV) nitrate test

Place 2 drops of the Ce(IV) reagent into a glass test tube, add 2 drops of acetonitrile and then 2 drops of an unknown (the sequence is important!). Shake the mixture. In the case of positive test the mixture color promptly changes from yellow to orange-red.

Note 1. Use only glass test tubes to perform the test. In case you need to wash the glass test tubes, carefully choose the appropriate solvent. Use caps to prevent the strong odor.

Note 2. Comparison with blank (no unknown) and reference (with ethanol) tests is recommended for adequate interpretation.

Note 3. Ce(IV) ions initially form brightly colored coordination compounds with alcohols. Complexes formed from primary or secondary alcohols react further (within 15 seconds to 1 hour) with the disappearance of the color.

2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH) test

Add only 1 drop of an unknown to $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of 95% ethanol in a plastic test tube. Add $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the DNPH reagent to the prepared solution. Shake the mixture and let it stand for 1-2 min. Observe formation of yellow to orange-red precipitate if the test is positive.

3.4. (4 pt) Write the reaction scheme for a positive 2,4-DNPH test with one of the compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{M}$.

Ferric hydroxamate test

Ask a lab assistant to light up your alcohol lamp. Mix $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $0.5\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ ethanolic hydroxylamine hydrochloride solution with 5 drops of $6\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ sodium hydroxide aqueous solution in a glass test tube. Add 1 drop of an unknown and use the alcohol lamp to heat the mixture to boiling while gently swirling the test tube to avoid splashes of the reaction mixture. Allow it to cool down slightly and add $2\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ HCl solution. Add 1 drop of 2.5% iron(III) chloride solution. Observe appearance of magenta color if the test is positive. Close the alcohol lamp with the cap when finished.

Note 1. Use glass test tubes only to perform the test; use the test tube holder when heating. In case you need to wash the glass test tubes, use an appropriate solvent. Stopper the test tubes with a green cap after completing the test to prevent a strong odor.

Note 2. Fe(III) ions form a colored 1:1 complex with hydroxamic acids (R-CO-NHOH).

3.5. (4 pt) Write the reaction scheme for a positive ferric hydroxamate test with one of the compounds $\mathbf{A}$-$\mathbf{M}$.

Note: After the STOP signal reattach the corresponding needles on the syringes with the unknown compounds, and place them into the plastic cup and leave them on the table.

problems.title: Acid-base indicator and its application for pH measurement
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1 (26 points / 13% of the total). Acid-base indicator and its application for pH measurement [printed as Task 1A]

Chemicals and Equipment (Task 1A)

I. Chemicals and materials (the actual labeling for each is given in bold font)

$$\begin{array}{l|c} & \text{Hazard Statements} \\ \hline \textbf{Instrument check solution}\text{, 80 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \\ 2.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\ \textbf{Methyl orange indicator solution}\text{, 30 cm}^3\text{ in a wide mouth glass bottle} & \text{H301} \\ 1.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\ \textbf{Bromothymol blue indicator solution}\text{, 30 cm}^3\text{ in a wide mouth glass bottle} & \\ \textbf{Methyl red indicator solution}\text{, 10 cm}^3\text{ in a wide mouth glass bottle} & \text{H225-H319-H371} \\ 1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\ \textbf{HCl}\text{, 30 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \text{H290-H314-H335} \\ 1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\ \textbf{NaOH}\text{, 30 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \text{H290-H314} \\ \text{buffer }\textbf{solution A}\text{, 110 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \\ \textbf{Unknown solution X}\text{, 50 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \\ \textbf{Unknown solution Y}\text{, 50 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \\ \textbf{Unknown solution Z}\text{, 50 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \end{array}$$

II. Equipment and labwares

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \textbf{Shared Equipment} & \textbf{Quantity} \\ \hline \text{UV-Visible spectrophotometer} & \text{1 per 2 students} \\ \hline \textbf{Personal Labwares} & \textbf{Quantity} \\ \hline \text{Beaker, 25 cm}^3 & 2 \\ \text{Volumetric flask, 25.00 cm}^3 & 9 \\ \text{Measuring pipette, 2.00 cm}^3 & 2 \\ \text{Measuring cylinder, 10.0 cm}^3 & 3 \\ \text{Pasteur pipette} & 6 \\ \text{Rubber bulb for Pasteur pipette} & 6 \\ \text{Pipette filler bulb (3-way)} & 1 \\ \text{Pipette tray} & 1 \\ \text{Test tube (13 x 100 mm)} & 6 \\ \text{Test tube rack} & 1 \\ \text{Plastic cuvette, optical path length = 1.00 cm} & 1 \\ \text{Waste bottle, 1 dm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Sticker label set in a zipped bag} & 1 \end{array}$$

Acid-base indicators are weak acids (or bases) that exhibit different colors when they are present in solution as their acidic form (HIn, color 1) or as their basic form ($\ce{In-}$, color 2). They undergo the following reaction in dilute aqueous solution.

$$\ce{HIn <=> H+ + In-}$$

As the pH of a solution containing the indicator changes, the equilibrium shown above will be driven either towards reactants (HIn), or products ($\ce{In-}$) causing the solution color to change depending on the concentration of each form present. In strongly acidic solution, most of the indicator will be present in the HIn form (color 1) and in strongly basic solutions, most of the indicator will be in the $\ce{In-}$ form (color 2). At intermediate pH values, the solution color will be a mix of color 1 (absorption at wavelength 1) and color 2 (absorption at wavelength 2), depending on the relative amounts of HIn and $\ce{In-}$ present.

By monitoring the absorbance values at two wavelengths, the concentrations of HIn and $\ce{In-}$ can be calculated by using the following expressions.

$$\begin{aligned} A^{\lambda1}_\mathrm{total} &= A^{\lambda1}_\mathrm{HIn} + A^{\lambda1}_\mathrm{In^-} \\ &= \varepsilon^{\lambda1}_\mathrm{HIn}\, b[\mathrm{HIn}] + \varepsilon^{\lambda1}_\mathrm{In^-}\, b[\mathrm{In^-}] \\ A^{\lambda2}_\mathrm{total} &= A^{\lambda2}_\mathrm{HIn} + A^{\lambda2}_\mathrm{In^-} \\ &= \varepsilon^{\lambda2}_\mathrm{HIn}\, b[\mathrm{HIn}] + \varepsilon^{\lambda2}_\mathrm{In^-}\, b[\mathrm{In^-}] \end{aligned}$$

where $b$ is pathlength of solution and $\varepsilon$ is the molar absorptivity.

At a certain pH value, the relative amounts of HIn and $\ce{In-}$ in solution are related to the acid dissociation constant ($K_\mathrm{a}$) of the indicator, as shown in the following equation.

$$K_\mathrm{a} = \frac{[\mathrm{H^+}][\mathrm{In^-}]}{[\mathrm{HIn}]}$$

Therefore, for a given pH value, acid dissociation constant ($K_\mathrm{a}$) of the indicator can be calculated when the relative amounts of HIn and $\ce{In-}$ in solution are known.

Experimental Set-up

Instructions for using a spectrophotometer

1. Set a spectrophometer to measure the absorbance at the desired wavelength following the procedure shown in the diagram.
2. Wipe the outside of a cuvette containing distilled water and insert the cuvette into the sample compartment.
3. Adjust the zero absorbance using water.
4. Remove the cuvette, replace water in the cuvette by sample solution to be analyzed. Make sure to tap out any bubbles and wipe the outside of the cuvette before placing the cuvette into the sample compartment.
5. Read the absorbance value of the sample.

Note: When changing the wavelength, make sure to adjust zero absorbance using “water”.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2017-1-fig2.png

General Information

In $0.1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ HCl, indicators are in the acidic form (HIn) only.

In $0.1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH, indicators are in the basic form ($\ce{In-}$) only.

There will be no mark for the answer in the dotted line box.

NOTE: Students are suggested to check the spectrophotometer before use by measuring the absorbance values of the instrument check solution at two different wavelengths, i.e., 430 and 620 nm.

Record the absorbance values of the instrument check solution

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} & A\ (\text{at }430\ \mathrm{nm}) & A\ (\text{at }620\ \mathrm{nm}) \\ \hline \text{Measured value} & & \\ \text{Guided value} & 0.220-0.260 & 0.450-0.510 \end{array}$$

In case that the measured values are within the guided values, students can proceed with further experiments. If not, students can ask for assistance.

Part a

Absorbance measurement of an acid-base indicator (methyl orange) in strong acid and strong base

1. Pipette $1.50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $2.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ methyl orange indicator solution into a $25.00\text{-}\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask, add $2.5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ HCl into the flask and make up to the volume using distilled water. Record the absorbance at 470 and 520 nm.
2. Pipette $2.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $2.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ methyl orange indicator solution into a $25.00\text{-}\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask, add $2.5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH into the flask and make up to the volume using distilled water. Record the absorbance at 470 and 520 nm.
3. Calculate the molar absorptivities at 470 and 520 nm of acidic and basic forms of methyl orange.

a2) (2 pt) Calculate the molar absorptivities of the acidic form and basic form of methyl orange (unit, $\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$).

The molar absorptivities of methyl orange are as follows: (unit, $\mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$)

Part b

Absorbance measurement of an acid-base indicator (bromothymol blue) in buffer solution

Bromothymol blue is an acid-base indicator which shows yellow color when it is present as an acidic form (HIn) and it shows blue color when it is present as a basic form ($\ce{In-}$). The absorption maximum of the bromothymol blue in the acidic form is at 430 nm and that in the basic form is at 620 nm. The molar absorptivities of bromothymol blue in the acidic form are $16{,}600\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at 430 nm and $0\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at 620 nm. The molar absorptivities of bromothymol blue in the basic form are $3{,}460\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at 430 nm and $38{,}000\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at 620 nm.

1. Pipette $1.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1.00\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ bromothymol blue indicator solution into a $25.00\text{-}\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask, and make up to the volume using solution A. (Note: solution A is a buffer solution pH = 7.00)
2. Record the absorbance at 430 and 620 nm.

Part c

Determination of solution pH by using acid-base indicator (methyl red)

Methyl red is an acid-base indicator which shows reddish-pink color when it is present as an acidic form (HIn) and it shows yellow color when it is present as a basic form ($\ce{In-}$). The molar absorptivities of methyl red in the acidic form are $9{,}810\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at 470 nm and $21{,}500\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at 520 nm. The molar absorptivities of methyl red in the basic form are $12{,}500\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at 470 nm and $1{,}330\ \mathrm{dm^3\,mol^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$ at 520 nm. The $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}$ of methyl red is 4.95.

problems.problem:
Practical problem 2 (26 points / 13% of the total). Calcium iodate [printed as Task 1B]

Chemicals and Equipment (Task 1B)

I. Chemicals and materials (the actual labeling for each is given in bold font)

$$\begin{array}{l|c} & \text{Health Statements} \\ \hline \textbf{Solution A (KIO}_\mathbf{3}\textbf{ 10.7042 g in 5.00 dm}^\mathbf{3}\textbf{)}\text{, 60 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \text{H272-H315-H319-H335} \\ \textbf{Solution B}\text{ (Saturated Ca(IO}_3\text{)}_2\text{ solution), 50 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \text{H272-H315-H319-H335} \\ \textbf{Solution C}\text{ (Saturated Ca(IO}_3\text{)}_2\text{ in unknown dilute KIO}_3\text{ solution), 50 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \text{H272-H315-H319-H335} \\ \text{Solution of }\textbf{Na}_\mathbf{2}\textbf{S}_\mathbf{2}\textbf{O}_\mathbf{3}\text{ 200 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \\ \textbf{KI 10\% (w/v)}\text{, 100 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \text{H300+H330-H312-H315-H319-H335} \\ \textbf{HCl 1 mol dm}^\mathbf{-3}\text{, 100 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic bottle} & \text{H290-H314-H335} \\ \textbf{Starch solution 0.1\% (w/v)}\text{, 30 cm}^3\text{ in a dropping glass bottle} & \\ \textbf{Distilled water}\text{, 500 cm}^3\text{ in a }\textbf{wash bottle} & \\ \textbf{Distilled water}\text{, 1000 cm}^3\text{ in a plastic }\textbf{gallon} & \end{array}$$

II. Equipment and labwares

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \textbf{Personal Labwares} & \textbf{Quantity} \\ \hline \text{Beaker, 100 cm}^3 & 2 \\ \text{Beaker, 250 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Erlenmeyer flask, 125 cm}^3 & 9 \\ \text{Transfer pipette, 5.00 cm}^3 & 2 \\ \text{Transfer pipette, 10.00 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Measuring cylinder, 10.0 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Measuring cylinder, 25.0 cm}^3 & 2 \\ \text{Pasteur pipette} & 1 \\ \text{Rubber bulb for Pasteur pipette} & 1 \\ \text{Glass funnel, 7.5 cm diameter} & 2 \\ \text{Plastic funnel, 5.5 cm diameter} & 1 \\ \text{Filter paper in a zipped bag} & 3 \\ \text{Burette, 50.0 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Burette stand and clamp} & 1 \\ \text{O-ring with bosshead} & 2 \end{array}$$

Calcium iodate is an inorganic salt composed of calcium and iodate ions. $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$ is sparingly soluble in water. Equilibrium is established between the undissolved salt and saturated solution of the salt.

$$\ce{Ca(IO3)2}_{(\mathrm{s})} \ce{<=>} \ce{Ca^{2+}}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + 2\,\ce{IO3^-}_{(\mathrm{aq})}$$

Titration data will be used to determine the concentration of iodate ions in a saturated solution of $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$ and then to determine the value of $K_\mathrm{sp}$ for $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$.

The concentration of iodate ion will be determined by titration with a standard solution of sodium thiosulfate ($\ce{Na2S2O3}$), in the presence of potassium iodide (KI). Starch will be used as an indicator.

Part a is associated with the standardization of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$. Part b is the determination of $K_\mathrm{sp}$ for $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$.

In Part C, solid $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$ is dissolved in an unknown dilute $\ce{KIO3}$ solution. After standing for 3 days, equilibrium is also established between the undissolved salt and saturated solution of the salt. The concentration of iodate ion will be determined using the same titrimetric method, and then used to calculate the concentration of the dilute $\ce{KIO3}$ solution.

Part a

Standardization of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$

1. Fill the burette with $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution.
2. Pipette $10.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of standard $\ce{KIO3}$ solution (provided as solution A, $\ce{KIO3}$ 10.7042 g in $5.00\ \mathrm{dm^3}$) into an Erlenmeyer flask. Add $10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of 10%(w/v) KI and $10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ HCl into a flask. The solution should turn dark brown as $\ce{I2}$ is formed.
3. Titrate with $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution until the solution has turned pale yellow. Add $2\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of 0.1%(w/v) starch solution. The solution should turn dark blue. Titrate carefully to the colorless endpoint. Record the volume of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution.

a1) (1 pt) Balance relevant chemical equations.

$$\ldots\ \ce{IO3^-}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + \ldots\ \ce{I^-}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + \ldots\ \ce{H3O^+}_{(\mathrm{aq})} \ce{->} \ldots\ \ce{I2}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + \ldots\ \ce{H2O}_{(\mathrm{l})}$$

$$\ldots\ \ce{I2}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + \ldots\ \ce{S2O3^{2-}}_{(\mathrm{aq})} \ce{->} \ldots\ \ce{I^-}_{(\mathrm{aq})} + \ldots\ \ce{S4O6^{2-}}_{(\mathrm{aq})}$$

a2) (5 pt) Record volume of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution. (You do not need to fill in the entire table)

Part b

Determination of $K_\mathrm{sp}$ of $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$

1. You are provided with the filtrate of the filtered saturated solution of $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$. (Solution B)
2. Pipette $5.00\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of the filtrate into an Erlenmeyer flask. Add $10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of 10% (w/v) KI and $10\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ HCl into a flask.
3. Titrate with $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution until the solution has turned pale yellow. Add $2\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ 0.1% (w/v) starch solution. The solution should turn dark blue. Titrate carefully to the colorless endpoint. Record the volume of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution.

b1) (6 pt) Record volume of $\ce{Na2S2O3}$ solution. (You do not need to fill in the entire table)

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c} & \text{Titration no.} & & \\ & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ \hline \text{Initial reading of the burette of Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3\text{ solution, cm}^3 & & & \\ \text{Final reading of the burette of Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3\text{ solution, cm}^3 & & & \\ \text{Consumed volume of Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3\text{ solution, cm}^3 & & & \end{array}$$

b2) (1 pt) Calculate the concentration of the $\ce{IO3-}$ solution.

Concentration of $\ce{IO3-}$, $\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$: …… (answer in 4 digits after decimal point)

b3) (2 pt) Calculate value of $K_\mathrm{sp}$ for $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$.

$K_\mathrm{sp}$ for $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$ = …… (answer in 3 significant figures)

(If the student cannot find $K_\mathrm{sp}$, use the value of $7\times10^{-7}$ for further calculations.)

Part c

Determination of concentration of unknown dilute $\ce{KIO3}$ solution

1. You are provided with the filtrate of the filtered saturated solution of $\ce{Ca(IO3)2}$ dissolved in the unknown dilute $\ce{KIO3}$ (provided as solution C).

problems.title: Elaborating Carbon Framework
problems.problem:
Practical problem 3 (24 points / 14% of the total). Elaborating Carbon Framework [printed as Task 2]

Chemicals and Equipment (Task 2)

I. Chemicals and materials

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} \textbf{Chemicals} & \textbf{Labeled as} & \textbf{Health Statements} \\ \hline \textbf{3-Pentanone (MW 86.13)}\text{, }{\sim}0.86\text{ g}^{\mathrm{b}}\text{ in a vial} & \textbf{A} & \text{H225-H319-H335-H336} \\ \boldsymbol{p}\textbf{-chlorobenzaldehyde (MW140.57)}\text{, }{\sim}3.5\text{ g}^{\mathrm{c}}\text{ in a vial} & \textbf{B} & \text{H302-H315-H319-H335} \\ \textbf{Ethanol}\text{, 200 cm}^3\text{ in a wash-bottle} & \textbf{Ethanol} & \text{H225-H319} \\ \text{2 mol dm}^{-3}\ \textbf{NaOH}\text{ solution in water (}\textbf{labelled as 2N NaOH}\text{), 25 cm}^3\text{ in a bottle} & \textbf{2N NaOH} & \text{H290-H314} \end{array}$$

b You will need to weigh the vial containing 3-pentanone right before using. The exact value can be calculated based on the information given on the label.

c The exact value is indicated on the label.

II. Equipment and labwares

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \textbf{Shared equipment} & \textbf{Quantity} \\ \hline \text{Balance} & \text{Shared 12 per room} \\ \text{Water aspirator} & \text{Shared 2 per bench} \\ \text{Foam bucket filled with ice} & \text{Shared 1 per row (Refill could be requested)} \\ \hline \textbf{Personal Equipment} & \textbf{Quantity} \\ \hline \text{Hotplate stirrer with temperature probe} & 1 \\ \text{Stand} & 1 \\ \text{Clamps} & 2 \\ \text{100-cm}^3\text{ Round bottom flask} & 1 \\ \text{Measuring cylinder, 25 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Measuring cylinder, 50 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Air condenser} & 1 \\ \text{Crystallizing dish, 250 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{125-cm}^3\text{ Erlenmeyer flask} & 2 \\ \text{Suction flask, 250 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Buchner funnel, 25 cm}^3 & 1 \\ \text{Watch glass} & 1 \\ \text{Pasteur pipettes (droppers)} & 5 \\ \text{Rubber bulbs} & 2 \\ \text{Suction rubber} & 1 \\ \text{Rubber support ring} & 1 \\ \text{Magnetic bar} & 1 \\ \text{Filter papers} & \text{3 (pack in 1 zipped bag)} \\ \text{Spatula} & 1 \\ \text{Stirring Rod} & 1 \\ \text{Forceps} & 1 \\ \text{Plastic joint clips} & 1 \\ \text{Wash Bottle (filled with EtOH)} & \text{1 (can be refilled)} \\ \text{Nitrile gloves} & \text{2 (exchange size if needed)} \\ \text{Towels} & 2 \\ \text{Paper clip} & 1 \\ \text{“Waste Task 2”, 500 cm}^3\text{-glass bottle} & 1 \\ \text{Vial labeled “Student code” for submitting product.} & 1 \\ \text{Goggles} & 1 \end{array}$$

The core structure of organic molecules is mostly based on carbon-carbon skeleton. Carbon-carbon bond formations have played a vital role in the construction of complex structures from smaller starting materials. Therefore, the synthetic transformations to efficiently achieve carbon-carbon bond formation has long been of interest. In this experiment, you are required to transform commercially available $p$-chlorobenzaldehyde and 3-pentanone to a more elaborated structure.

Important Notes:
• Ethanol can be refilled with no penalty.
• All weighing processes require verification from lab supervisor. The supervisor will need to sign in the student’s answer sheet for grading. No mark will be given for unverified values.
• Total of 18 points of this exam score will be based on the quality and quantity of the product submitted. We could not give any score on this part if the product is not submitted for grading.
• $^1$H-NMR and melting point determination techniques will be used by the grader to verify the quality of your product.

Part a

1. Take the vial containing 3-pentanone ($\mathbf{A}$) (Code Axxx, For example: A305) and unwrap the parafilm. Weigh the vial with caps. Record the weight in the answer sheet question a1.
2. Setup a water bath by filling water in the $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$-crystallizing dish and heat to $55\pm2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Add paper clip into the water bath and let it stir so that the heat could be distributed evenly.
3. Ensure a magnetic stirring bar is in the $100\text{-}\mathrm{cm^3}$ round bottom flask. Transfer the pre-weighed 3-pentanone (labeled as $\mathbf{A}$) and $p$-chlorobenzaldehyde (labeled as $\mathbf{B}$) to the flask. Add $50\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ ethanol to the mixture and swirl to dissolve.
4. Measure $15\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of $2\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ NaOH (labeled as 2N NaOH) using a measuring cylinder and add to the reaction mixture. Be careful not to wet the ground joint with NaOH solution.
5. Setup the reaction as shown in Figure 1. The reaction flask is placed in the $55\pm2\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ water bath. Attach the air condenser to the reaction flask with plastic joint clip. Heat the reaction mixture while stirring for 30 minutes using the water bath.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2017-3-fig1.png

Figure 1: Set up needed for heating the reaction with water bath.

6. Remove the reaction flask from the water bath. (Be careful! The flask might be hot.) Place the flask on the rubber supporting ring.
7. (Important) Detach the probe from the hotplate/stirrer to avoid over-heating of the hotplate in the recrystallizing steps. After you detach the probe, inform the supervisor to check and submit the probe to the supervisor.
8. Prepare the ice bath by replacing the warm water in the $250\ \mathrm{cm^3}$-crystalizing dish with ice and small amount of water. Place the reaction flask on the ice bath to cool down the reaction. Solid should be observed. (Suggestion: If you do not observe any solid within 5 minutes, you may use a stirring rod to scratch the side of the flask. This could induce precipitation.)
9. Keep the mixture cool for approximately 20 minutes to allow complete precipitation.
10. Set up the suction filtration equipment (Figure 2). Connect the suction flask to the water aspirator. Place a Buchner funnel fitted with a rubber adapter onto the suction flask. Place a filter paper at the center of the funnel. Filter the precipitate $via$ suction filtration and wash the precipitate with small amount of cold ethanol. Let air suck through the precipitates for 2-3 minutes to dry the product.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2017-3-fig2.png

Figure 2: Set up needed for suction filtration.

11. Disconnect the vacuum (before turning off the water aspirator). Bring your equipment back to your space and keep the common area clean. Collect the crude precipitates from the filter paper and transfer to the Erlenmeyer flask. Careful not to scrape the paper too hard as you may obtain small pieces of paper as contaminant. Student may use Ethanol to rinse the Buchner funnel.
12. Place ethanol in a separate Erlenmeyer flask and heat it gently on a hotplate. (Student may set the temperature mark at $100\text{-}120\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) Before heating, please make sure that the temperature probe is detached from the hotplate.
13. Recrystallize the product from hot ethanol. You can follow the procedure below.

Add small amount of hot ethanol to the flask containing crude solid while swirling. Continue addition of hot ethanol (swirling after each addition) until the solid is completely dissolved. During the dissolution process, keep the flask hot at all times by resting it on the hotplate. Be careful that the flask may be hot. You may use paper towels or towels provided to wrap around the flask while swirling. Once the dissolution is complete, set the flask containing the dissolved compound on a benchtop and let the flask cool down to room temperature without disturbance. The crystalline product should be observed. If not, you may use the stirring rod to scratch the side of the flask to induce crystallization. Place the flask into the ice bath to complete crystallization.

14. Filter the recrystallized product $via$ suction filtration (See step 10 for suction filtration protocol) and wash the product with small amount of cold ethanol. Let air suck through the precipitates for 2-3 minutes. Disconnect the vacuum. Let the purified product air-dry on the benchtop for at least 15 minutes.
15. Weigh the vial (without cap) labeled with your student code provided. Record the value in the answer sheet question a1.
16. Transfer the recrystallized product to the pre-weighed vial. Determine and record the mass of the purified product in the answer sheet question a1.
17. Fill the information on the label of the product vial. Place the product-containing vial on the benchtop. The supervisor will pick up your vial and sign on your answer sheet question b after the “Stop command”. The student also must sign the answer sheet question b for grading. Once both supervisor and student sign, place the vial into a zipped bag and submitted for grading.

These following items should be left on your bench:
• The exam/answer booklet (this booklet) placed in an exam envelope
• The vial labeled “Student Code” with filled information

Supervisor will place a label here when randomly distributed the compounds:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \text{Axxx (For example: A567) =} & \text{Code of vial containing 3-pentanone} \\ \text{Tared (w/caps):} & \text{Mass of (vial + label + caps) }\textbf{before}\text{ adding 3-pentanone} \\ \text{Bxxx (For example: B567) =} & \text{Code of vial containing }p\text{-chlorobenzaldehyde} \\ \text{Net:} & \text{Mass of }p\text{-chlorobenzaldehyde} \end{array}$$

a1) (2 pt) Use the information provided in the label above along with your experimental data for your calculation. Write down all the results in this Table.

problems.title: Haloform reaction with bleach
problems.problem:
Practical problem 1 (50 points / 14% of the total). Haloform reaction with bleach [printed as Problem P1]

Chemicals for Problem P1 (in white basket if not stated otherwise)

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} \text{Chemicals} & \text{Labelled as} & \text{GHS hazard statements} \\ \hline \textbf{Ethanol}\text{, 100 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in wash bottle (bench)} & \textbf{Ethanol} & \text{H225, H319} \\ \textbf{2-Acetonaphthone}\text{:} & & \\ \quad\text{ca. 0.002 g in glass vial, standard for TLC} & \textbf{Standard A} & \text{H302, H315, H319, H335, H411} \\ \quad\text{0.500 g in glass vial} & \textbf{Reactant A} & \\ \textbf{2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine}\text{, containing 33\% (w/w) of water, 0.300 g in glass vial} & \textbf{DNPH} & \text{H228, H302} \\ \text{Bleach solution, containing 4.7\% of }\textbf{NaClO}\text{, 13.5 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in amber glass bottle} & \textbf{Bleach} & \text{H290, H314, H400} \\ \textbf{Ethyl acetate}\text{, 15 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in amber glass bottle} & \textbf{EtOAc} & \text{H225, H319, H336} \\ \textbf{Eluent}\text{ for thin layer chromatography, hexanes/ethyl acetate 4:1 (v/v), 5 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in amber glass bottle} & \textbf{TLC eluent} & \text{H225, H304, H315, H336, H411}^{*} \\ \text{5\% }\ce{Na2CO3}\text{, aqueous solution, 20 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in plastic bottle} & \textbf{5\% }\ce{Na2CO3} & \text{H319} \\ \text{20\% }\textbf{HCl}\text{, aqueous solution, 15 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in plastic bottle} & \textbf{20\% HCl} & \text{H290, H314, H319, H335 and others} \end{array}$$

$^{*}$ The GHS hazard statements for hexanes.

Equipment for Problem P1 (in white basket if not stated otherwise)

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Shared equipment} & \text{Quantity} \\ \hline \text{UV lamp (hood)} & \text{1 for up to 12} \\ \text{Vacuum source (plastic stopcock with vacuum hose, bench)} & \text{1 for 2} \\ \hline \text{Personal equipment} & \\ \hline \text{Hotplate stirrer (bench) with:} & \text{1 (each)} \\ \quad\text{Temperature probe,} & \\ \quad\text{Crystallizing dish, with metallic clip} & \\ \text{Laboratory stand (bench) with:} & \text{1 (each)} \\ \quad\text{Clamp holder with small clamp} & \\ \quad\text{Clamp holder with large clamp} & \\ \textbf{Organic waste}\text{ plastic bottle (bench)} & 1 \\ \text{Open metal ring} & 1 \\ \text{Round bottom flask, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{, with magnetic stir bar} & 1 \\ \text{Measuring cylinder, 10 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Reflux condenser} & 1 \\ \text{Separatory funnel, 100 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{, with stopper} & 1 \\ \text{Erlenmeyer flask without ground joint, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Erlenmeyer flask without ground joint, 25 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Erlenmeyer flask with ground joint, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Glass funnel} & 1 \\ \text{Suction flask, 100 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Rubber adapter for filter funnel} & 1 \\ \text{Fritted glass filter funnel, porosity }\textbf{S2}\text{ (white label)} & 1 \\ \text{Fritted glass filter funnel, porosity }\textbf{S3}\text{ (orange label)} & 1 \\ \text{Glass beaker, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{, with Petri dish lid} & 1 \\ \text{Glass beaker, 150 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{TLC graduated capillary spotter, 5 }\mathrm{\mu l} & 3 \\ \text{Zipped bag with 5 pH indicator strips and 1 pH scale} & 1 \\ \text{Zipped bag with 2 TLC plates} & 1 \\ \text{Glass Pasteur pipette} & 4 \\ \text{Rubber bulb} & 1 \\ \text{Glass vial labelled }\textbf{Student code B}\text{ for the product of the haloform reaction} & 1 \\ \text{Glass vial labelled }\textbf{Student code C}\text{ for the product of the reaction with Brady's reagent} & 1 \end{array}$$

Chemical test reactions have been developed as a means of identifying functional groups in unknown compounds. In this task, you will explore two examples of chemical test reactions on a preparatory scale, starting from (2-naphthyl)ethanone ($\mathbf{A}$, 2-acetonaphthone):

• The haloform reaction is a transformation typical for methyl ketones which react with basic aqueous hypohalite solution and provide a carboxylic acid (product $\mathbf{B}$) and a haloform (trihalomethane).
• The reaction of Brady's reagent (acidic solution of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine) with the carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone results in the formation of an orange hydrazone precipitate (product $\mathbf{C}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2018-1-fig1.png

P1.1 (4 pt) Draw the structures of products $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

Notes:
• The total score will be based on the $R_\mathrm{f}$ values of compounds $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ calculated from the submitted TLC plate 1 and on the quality and quantity of the submitted products $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.
• The quality of your products will be graded based on the TLC and melting points.
• The amount of the provided hypochlorite solution is not sufficient to convert all reactant $\mathbf{A}$ to product $\mathbf{B}$. You will recover the residual reactant $\mathbf{A}$ by an acid-base extraction and isolate it after the reaction with Brady's reagent as hydrazone $\mathbf{C}$. The grading is based on the combined yield of products $\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{C}$.

Procedure

I. Haloform reaction

1. Turn on the stirrer and adjust the speed to 540 rpm. Immerse a temperature probe, resting the wire on the upper clamp into the bath almost to the bottom and set the temperature to 80 °C.
2. Transfer the 0.500 g of 2-acetonaphthone from the vial labelled Reactant A into a 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ round bottom flask that contains a magnetic stir bar. Measure 3 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol (from the wash bottle) in a measuring cylinder and use it to transfer the remaining reactant $\mathbf{A}$ quantitatively into the round bottom flask using a glass Pasteur pipette.
3. Place the round bottom flask into the hot water bath. Attach an air reflux condenser (water connection is not needed) and secure it in the upper part by a loosely attached large clamp, as shown in Figure 1. Let compound $\mathbf{A}$ dissolve with stirring.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2018-1-fig2.png

Figure 1. Setup for heating the reaction mixture in a water bath.

4. When the bath temperature reaches 75 °C, slowly add all the NaClO solution (Bleach) to the reaction mixture through the top opening of the condenser using a small glass funnel. Heat the reaction mixture with stirring for 60 minutes between 75 and 80 °C.
5. Then turn off the heating of the hotplate stirrer. Loosen the upper clamp a bit and lift the reaction flask over the water bath. (Caution! Touch only the clamps, the flask is hot.) Allow the reaction mixture to cool down for 15 minutes.

II. Workup of the reaction mixture

1. Place a separatory funnel into a metal ring and place a 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ Erlenmeyer flask without a ground joint under it. Using a glass funnel, pour the cooled reaction mixture into the separatory funnel. Remove the stir bar from the glass funnel with tweezers. Measure 5 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethyl acetate (EtOAc) and use it to rinse the reaction flask.. Add the washings into the separatory funnel using a glass Pasteur pipette.
2. Perform the extraction. Allow the layers to separate. Collect the aqueous layer into the 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ Erlenmeyer flask without a ground joint. Using a small glass funnel, pour the organic layer through the top neck into the 25 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ Erlenmeyer flask. Keep both phases!
3. Using a small funnel, pour the aqueous phase from the 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ Erlenmeyer flask back to the separatory funnel. Measure another 5 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethyl acetate and repeat the extraction (step No. II.2). Combine the organic phases together in the 25 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ Erlenmeyer flask. Keep both phases!
4. Prepare your TLC plate. Check it before use. Unused damaged plates will be replaced upon request without penalty. Use a pencil to draw the start line and mark the positions for spotting the samples. Write number 1 in a circle and your student code on the top of the TLC plate as shown in Figure 2. Dissolve the given sample of 2-acetonaphthone in a small vial (Standard A) in ca. 2 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol (about 1 full glass Pasteur pipette). Mark three spot positions and label them $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{O1}$, and $\mathbf{O2}$. Spot 1 $\mathrm{\mu l}$ (one mark of the 5 $\mathrm{\mu l}$ capillary spotter) of standard $\mathbf{A}$ and the combined organic phase from step II.3 ($\mathbf{O1}$). You will add spot $\mathbf{O2}$ later.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2018-1-fig3.png

Figure 2. Instructions for the TLC plate preparation.

5. Extract the combined organic phases twice with 5 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 5% $\ce{Na2CO3}$ solution. Collect the aqueous phase into the same 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ Erlenmeyer flask without a ground joint containing the aqueous phase from the first extraction.
6. Wash the organic phase in the funnel with 5 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of deionized water. Add the aqueous phase to the combined aqueous extracts. Pour the organic layer ($\mathbf{O2}$) through the top neck into a 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ ground-joint Erlenmeyer flask. Spot 1 $\mathrm{\mu l}$ of the solution $\mathbf{O2}$ on your TLC plate prepared in step II.4 (Plate 1).
7. Perform a TLC analysis. Take a 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ beaker and load it with ca. 2 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the TLC eluent. Insert the TLC plate, cover the beaker with a Petri dish and let the eluent reach approximately 0.5 cm bellow the top edge of the plate. Using tweezers, take the TLC plate out, draw the eluent front line and let the plate air-dry. Place the TLC plate under the UV lamp in the hood. With a pencil, circle all the visualized spots and calculate the $R_\mathrm{f}$ values of reactant $\mathbf{A}$ and product $\mathbf{B}$. Store your TLC plate in a plastic bag.

Note 1: Product $\mathbf{B}$ may tail on the TLC plate. Therefore, avoid excessive loading of the sample.

Note 2: In some cases, two additional spots of side products of a very low intensity may be seen in combined organic phase $\mathbf{O1}$ and $\mathbf{O2}$. In this case, calculate the $R_\mathrm{f}$ value for the most intense spot(s).

Note 3: If the organic layer $\mathbf{O2}$ still contains both starting material $\mathbf{A}$ and product $\mathbf{B}$, repeat the extraction with the $\ce{Na2CO3}$ solution and water (steps No. II.5 and II.6). In this case, submit also another TLC plate after the repeated extraction (Plate 2), spotting only standard $\mathbf{A}$ and organic phase $\mathbf{O2}$. Mark number 2 in a circle and your student code on the top of this TLC plate. Use a fresh batch of eluent to develop TLC Plate 2.

P1.2 (16 pt) Answer the following questions about your Plate(s). From Plate 1, calculate the $R_\mathrm{f}$ values of standard $\mathbf{A}$ and product $\mathbf{B}$. Provide the results rounded to 2 decimal places.

Based on the TLC analysis, your organic layer $\mathbf{O1}$ contains:
• Starting material $\mathbf{A}$: □ YES □ NO
• Product $\mathbf{B}$: □ YES □ NO

Based on the TLC analysis, your final organic layer $\mathbf{O2}$ contains:
• Starting material $\mathbf{A}$: □ YES □ NO
• Product $\mathbf{B}$: □ YES □ NO

Calculation of the $R_\mathrm{f}(\mathbf{A})$

Calculation of the $R_\mathrm{f}(\mathbf{B})$

III. Reaction with Brady's reagent

Attention: Use gloves! Brady's reagent stains skin and all surfaces. Wash any spots immediately with ethanol! Change your gloves if necessary.

Preheat the water bath to 80 °C. Insert a magnetic stir bar into the 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ ground-joint Erlenmeyer flask containing the organic phase $\mathbf{O2}$ from step II.6 and add 0.300 g of 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (DNPH). In a graduated cylinder, measure 10 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol. Using a glass Pasteur pipette, rinse the glass vial with $5\times2\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol to transfer all of the DNPH into the Erlenmeyer flask. Place the Erlenmeyer flask into the hot water bath, attach a reflux condenser (similar setup as in Figure 1) rinsed with ethanol. Through the top opening of the condenser, add 3 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 20% HCl using a funnel and stir the reaction mixture at 80 °C for 2 minutes. Fine orange crystals of product $\mathbf{C}$ start to form. Then turn off the heating of the hotplate stirrer. Lift the reaction flask above the water bath. (Caution! Touch only the clamps, the flask is hot.) Allow the reaction mixture to cool down for 15 min and then place it into a cold water bath (prepared by pouring cold tap water in a 150 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ beaker).

IV. Isolation of the products

1. Check the pH of the combined aqueous phase from step No. II.6. Acidify it by carefully adding 20% HCl solution, stirring the mixture with a glass rod (ca. 2 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the HCl solution should be required), to the final pH of 2 (check with pH indicator strips). A white precipitate of product $\mathbf{B}$ is formed.
2. Set up a vacuum filtration apparatus (Figure 3) using a glass fritted funnel with porosity S2 (with white label) and secure it to a laboratory stand with a small clamp. Connect the suction flask to the vacuum source. Pour the suspension of product $\mathbf{B}$ (step No. IV.1) into the fritted funnel, let the solid set down, and then open the vacuum valve. Caution: notify the lab assistant before and after handling the valve! Wash the solid twice with 6 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of deionized water, until the pH of the dropping filtrate is about 6. Let air suck through the precipitate for 5 minutes to pre-dry the product. Disconnect the vacuum source. Use the spatula to transfer white product $\mathbf{B}$ to a glass vial labelled Student code B and leave it uncovered on the bench to dry. Discard the filtrate to the sink drain and wash the suction flask.

Note: Be careful not to scratch the fritted glass into your product!

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2018-1-fig4.png

Figure 3. Setup for suction filtration.

3. Set up a vacuum filtration apparatus with a glass fritted funnel with porosity S3 (with an orange label) similarly as in IV.2. Pour the suspension of product $\mathbf{C}$ (step No. III) into the fritted funnel, wait for a minute, and then open the vacuum valve. Do NOT stir or scratch the solid with the spatula while filtering and washing, otherwise the solid may go through the filter. Wash the precipitate three times with 5 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of ethanol (15 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ in total) until neutral pH of the dropping filtrate is reached. Let air suck through the precipitate for 5 minutes. Disconnect the vacuum source. Use the spatula to transfer orange product $\mathbf{C}$ to a glass vial labelled Student code C and leave it uncovered on the bench to dry. Collect the filtrate into Organic waste bottle.

Note: If the product goes through the fritted funnel, filter the suspension once more. If the product still goes through, contact the lab assistant.

Your lab assistant will pick up following items and sign your answer sheet.
• Glass vials labelled Student code B and C with your products
• TLC plates in a zipped bag labelled with your Student code

[Points for the laboratory work: yield 20 pt, m.p. 10 pt.]

problems.title: A glowing clock reaction
problems.problem:
Practical problem 2 (80 points / 13% of the total). A glowing clock reaction [printed as Problem P2]

Chemicals for Problem P2 (in green basket)

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} \text{Chemicals} & \text{Labelled as} & \text{GHS hazard statements} \\ \hline 8\ \mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}\text{ }\textbf{luminol}\text{ in }0.4\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\text{ }\textbf{NaOH}\text{ aqueous solution, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in plastic bottle} & \textbf{Luminol in NaOH} & \text{H290, H315, H319} \\ 2.00\ \mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}\text{ }\ce{CuSO4}\text{ aqueous solution, 25 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in plastic bottle} & \textbf{Cu} & \text{Not hazardous} \\ 2.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\text{ }\ce{H2O2}\text{ aqueous solution, 12 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in small plastic bottle} & \ce{H2O2}\textbf{ conc.} & \text{H302, H315, H318} \\ 0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\text{ }\textbf{cysteine hydrochloride}\text{ aqueous solution, 12 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in small plastic bottle} & \textbf{Cys conc.} & \text{Not hazardous} \\ \textbf{Water}\text{, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in plastic bottle} & \textbf{Water} & \text{Not hazardous} \end{array}$$

Equipment for Problem P2 (in green basket if not stated otherwise)

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Personal equipment} & \text{Quantity} \\ \hline \text{Stopwatch} & 1 \\ \text{Digital thermometer and card with its calibration constant} & 1 \\ \text{Volumetric flask, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Bulb pipette, 5 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ (bench, in pipette stand)} & 1 \\ \text{Graduated pipette, 5 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ (bench, in pipette stand)} & 3 \\ \text{Graduated pipette, 1 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ (bench, in pipette stand)} & 2 \\ \text{Plastic bottle labelled }\ce{H2O2}\textbf{ dil.}\text{ for diluted stock solution of }\ce{H2O2}\text{, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Plastic bottle labelled }\textbf{Cys dil.}\text{ for diluted stock solution cysteine.HCl, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Black plastic test tube, 15 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Capless centrifuge tube, 1.5 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Plastic beaker, 25 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Erlenmeyer flask, 100 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \end{array}$$

Luminol is a well-known source of chemiluminescence. In the presence of a suitable redox catalyst, e.g. $\ce{Cu^{2+}}$, it may react with oxidizing agents, most commonly $\ce{H2O2}$, forming products in excited electronic states. These release the excess energy by the emission of blue light:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2018-2-fig1.png

The procedure may be modified into a clock reaction, in which the light appears after a certain induction time. By adding cysteine, Cu(II) is reduced to Cu(I) and captured in a Cu(I)–cysteine complex that does not facilitate the luminol oxidation. However, the inhibition is only temporary. A cycle of reactions fuelled by $\ce{H2O2}$ leads to the gradual oxidation of cysteine:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2018-2-fig2.png

Eventually, all cysteine is consumed, Cu(I) is reoxidized to Cu(II), and its catalytic activity is restored. This is indicated by a flash of blue chemiluminescence. The time it takes for the flash to appear can be used to study the rates of the Cu-catalyzed cysteine oxidation.

Procedure

Caution: Always keep all your solutions and pipettes away from hotplates!

Reasonable temperature changes are not a problem, because your results will be marked based on the actual reaction temperatures that you report. You will not lose any points if your data is recorded at various temperatures. However, you must avoid excessive heat, e.g. placing the solutions or the pipettes near a hotplate.

Note: Report all the values with the requested number of significant figures or decimal places. Excessive rounding may make it impossible to distinguish a correct answer from an incorrect one.

General structure of the experiment

In Part I, you will dilute two stock solutions that are provided as concentrates. In Part II, you will measure the reaction times of the clock reaction for two different concentration sets, as defined in the table below:

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \text{Volume in the black test tube} & & & \text{In the centrifuge tube} & \\ & \text{Water} & \text{Luminol in NaOH} & \text{Cys dil.} & \text{Cu} & \ce{H2O2}\text{ dil.} \\ \hline \text{Conc. set \#1} & 3.00\ \mathrm{cm^3} & 2.50\ \mathrm{cm^3} & 3.30\ \mathrm{cm^3} & 0.50\ \mathrm{cm^3} & 0.70\ \mathrm{cm^3} \\ \text{Conc. set \#2} & 3.30\ \mathrm{cm^3} & 2.50\ \mathrm{cm^3} & 3.30\ \mathrm{cm^3} & 0.50\ \mathrm{cm^3} & 0.40\ \mathrm{cm^3} \end{array}$$

It is recommended that before you start measuring the data to be graded, you should get familiar with the procedure in a trial run.

Because the reaction rate depends on temperature, you must record the actual temperatures in all replicates. The temperatures in the reaction mixtures should be measured IMMEDIATELY AFTER you have recorded the reaction time required to produce the blue flash.

In data evaluation, each temperature recorded from the thermometer's display must be corrected by summing it with the thermometer's calibration constant. This constant is printed on a piece of paper in the basket for Problem 2.

Then, each reaction time $t(x\ ^\circ\mathrm{C})$ observed at $x$ °C (corrected) must be converted to the time $t(25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C})$ that would be observed at 25 °C. This normalization of reaction times to 25 °C is a simple multiplication of $t(x\ ^\circ\mathrm{C})$ with a normalization coefficient $n_{x\to25}$:

$$t(25\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}) = n_{x\to25}\, t(x\ ^\circ\mathrm{C})$$

The values of the normalization coefficients $n_{x\to25}$ corresponding to various temperatures are listed in Table P2 at the end of this task.

I. Dilution of the concentrated stock solutions

Solutions of $\ce{H2O2}$ ($2.00\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) and cysteine ($0.100\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$) are provided as concentrates, labelled $\ce{H2O2}$ conc. and Cys conc. Using the 5 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ bulb pipette and the 50 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask, dilute 5.00 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of each to 50.00 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ with deionized water and store the diluted solution in the bottles labelled $\ce{H2O2}$ dil. and Cys dil.

For measuring the solution volumes in the following steps, assign one graduated pipette for each of the bottles. The 5 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ pipettes are for Luminol in NaOH, Cys dil., and Water. The 1 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ pipettes are for Cu ($2.00\ \mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}$) and $\ce{H2O2}$ dil.

II. The clock reaction procedure

Note: Read the entire Section II carefully before starting the experiment.

1. Place the black test tube inside the Erlenmeyer flask serving as a stand. Using the assigned pipettes, charge the test tube with the prescribed volumes of Water, Luminol in NaOH and Cys dil. solution.
2. Place the small centrifuge tube inside the small plastic beaker and charge it with the prescribed volumes of Cu solution and $\ce{H2O2}$ dil. solution.
3. Without delay, insert the small centrifuge tube inside the black test tube – gently, without mixing the two solutions!
4. Close the test tube with its screw-on cap. Make sure that the tube is closed tightly, because you will be shaking it. Caution: Do not force the cap beyond its end-point, because the tube will start leaking. If this happens, you must ask for a replacement immediately (penalty rules apply).
5. Have the stopwatch ready in your hand, in timing mode. The moment you begin shaking the test tube, start timing. You must shake vigorously during the initial 10 seconds, so that the two solutions mix perfectly. It is crucial that you do not cut down the shaking time.
6. Return the test tube into the Erlenmeyer flask, open the lid and watch the solution inside closely. It may help to shield away the daylight with your hand. Eventually, you will see a flash of blue light through the whole solution. At that moment, stop timing.
7. Immediately, insert the metal probe of the digital thermometer into the black test tube. Wait for the reading to stabilize (typically 10–30 s) and record the reaction time and the reaction temperature.
8. Using tweezers, remove the small centrifuge tube from the black test tube. After each experiment, empty and wash both tubes and dry them with paper wipes.

Measured data and their evaluation

P2.1 (30 pt) In the following table, record your experimental results for concentration set #1. To the displayed temperature add the thermometer's calibration constant. Look up the value of the normalization coefficient $n_{x\to25}$ for each temperature in Table P2 and calculate the reaction times normalized to 25 °C. In an unlikely case that your temperatures are not listed in Table P2, get the value of $n_{x\to25}$ from the lab assistant.

Note: Just as the tolerance for correct values in titration is $\pm0.1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, the tolerance for correct values of the normalized times in the concentration set #1 is $\pm2.3$ s.

(Use as many replicates as you consider necessary, you do not need to fill in all the rows. Points will be awarded for the accepted value only.)

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \text{Replicate} & \text{Reaction time [s]} & \text{Displayed temperature [°C]} & \text{Corrected temperature [°C]} & \text{Reaction time normalized to 25 °C [s]} \\ & & \text{1 decimal place} & \text{1 decimal place} & \text{1 decimal place} & \text{3 significant figures} \\ \hline \text{Conc. set \#1} & 1 & & & & \\ & 2 & & & & \\ & 3 & & & & \\ \hline & \text{Accepted value of the normalized reaction time for concentration set \#1} & & & & \end{array}$$

P2.2 (30 pt) In the following table, record your experimental results, the corrected temperature and calculate the reaction times normalized to 25 °C for concentration set #2.

Note: Just as the tolerance for correct values in titration is $\pm0.1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, the tolerance for the correct values of the normalized times in the concentration set #2 is $\pm3.0$ s.

(Use as many replicates as you consider necessary; you do not need to fill in all the rows. Points will be awarded for the accepted value only.)

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \text{Replicate} & \text{Reaction time [s]} & \text{Displayed temperature [°C]} & \text{Corrected temperature [°C]} & \text{Reaction time normalized to 25 °C [s]} \\ & & \text{1 decimal place} & \text{1 decimal place} & \text{1 decimal place} & \text{3 significant figures} \\ \hline \text{Conc. set \#2} & 1 & & & & \\ & 2 & & & & \\ & 3 & & & & \\ \hline & \text{Accepted value of the normalized reaction time for concentration set \#2} & & & & \end{array}$$

P2.3 (7 pt) Based on the procedure and on the concentrations of the stock solutions (specified in the list of chemicals and in Part I. of the Procedure), calculate the initial concentrations of cysteine, copper and $\ce{H2O2}$ in both concentration sets.

Express the accepted reaction times ($t_1$ and $t_2$) from P2.1 and P2.2 in minutes and calculate the corresponding reaction rates ($v_1$ and $v_2$), expressed as the rates of the consumption of the cysteine concentration, in $\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}\,min^{-1}}$. You can assume that the rate of cysteine consumption during the reaction is constant.

If you cannot find the reaction rates, use the value 11.50 for conc. set #1 and 5.500 for conc. set #2 in further calculations.

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} & \text{Initial concentrations } [\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}}] & & & \text{Accepted reaction time [min]} & \text{Reaction rate } [\mathrm{mmol\,dm^{-3}\,min^{-1}}] \\ & \text{3 significant figures} & & & \text{4 significant figures} & \text{4 significant figures} \\ & \text{Cysteine} & \text{Copper [Cu]} & \ce{H2O2} & & \\ \hline \text{Conc. set \#1} & & & & & \\ \text{Conc. set \#2} & & & & & \end{array}$$

P2.4 (3 pt) Assuming the rate equation can be expressed as

$$v = k\,[\ce{H2O2}]^{p}$$

use your experimental data to calculate the partial reaction order $p$ with respect to $\ce{H2O2}$. Write down your answer with 2 decimal places and show your calculation.

Chemicals for Problem P3 (in grey basket if not stated otherwise)

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c} \text{Chemicals} & \text{Labelled as} & \text{GHS hazard statements} \\ \hline \textbf{Sample of mineral water}\text{, 400 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in plastic bottle (bench)} & \textbf{Sample} & \text{Not hazardous} \\ 3\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\text{ }\ce{NH4Cl}\text{ / }3\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\text{ }\ce{NH3}\text{ solution in water, 15 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in plastic bottle} & \textbf{Buffer} & \text{H302, H319, H314, H400} \\ \textbf{NaCl}\text{, solid, 10 g in plastic bottle} & \textbf{NaCl} & \text{H319} \\ \textbf{Eriochrome black T}\text{, indicator mixture in plastic bottle} & \textbf{EBT} & \text{H319} \\ \textbf{Bromothymol blue}\text{, indicator solution in plastic bottle} & \textbf{BTB} & \text{H302, H315, H319} \\ 5.965\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\text{ }\textbf{disodium ethylenediamine tetraacetate}\text{ standard solution, 200 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in plastic bottle (bench)} & \textbf{EDTA} & \text{H302, H315, H319, H335} \\ 0.2660\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}\text{ }\textbf{NaOH}\text{ standard solution, 250 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ in plastic bottle (bench)} & \textbf{NaOH} & \text{H314} \\ \text{Strong }\textbf{acidic cation exchange resin}\text{, in }\ce{H+}\text{ form, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ of swollen material washed with deionized water in plastic bottle} & \textbf{Catex} & \text{H319} \end{array}$$

Equipment for Problem P3 (in grey basket if not stated otherwise)

$$\begin{array}{l|c} \text{Personal equipment} & \text{Quantity} \\ \hline \text{Laboratory stand (bench) with:} & \text{1 (each)} \\ \quad\text{White sheet of paper} & \\ \quad\text{Burette clamp} & \\ \quad\text{Burette, 25 }\mathrm{cm^3} & \\ \text{Bulb pipette, 50 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ (bench, in pipette stand)} & 1 \\ \text{Bulb pipette, 10 }\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ (bench, in pipette stand)} & 1 \\ \text{Glass funnel} & 1 \\ \text{Measuring cylinder, 5 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Titration flask (flat bottom flask), 250 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 2 \\ \text{Erlenmeyer flask, 250 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Fritted glass filter funnel, porosity }\textbf{S1}\text{ (blue label)} & 1 \\ \text{Glass beaker, 100 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 2 \\ \text{Glass beaker, 250 }\mathrm{cm^3} & 1 \\ \text{Plastic Pasteur pipette, narrow stem, nongraduated} & 2 \\ \text{Plastic Pasteur pipette, thick stem, graduated} & 1 \\ \text{Zipped bag with 5 pH indicator strips and 1 pH scale} & 1 \\ \text{Zipped bag with 5 absorbing paper strips} & 1 \\ \textbf{Waste catex}\text{ plastic bottle (bench)} & 1 \end{array}$$

Many mineral and thermal water springs are registered in Slovakia. Mineral waters with a balanced composition and natural or modified carbon dioxide content are sold for daily consumption. These waters do not contain nitrites, nitrates, phosphates, fluorides and sulfides and are also free of iron and manganese.

The mass concentration of the most important ions is reported on the packaging.

Your task is to identify the trade brand (from Table P3.1) of your mineral water sample.

Note: $\ce{CO2}$ has been removed from the sample.

Table P3.1. Mass concentrations of ions in selected Slovak mineral waters. (As reported by the supplier.)

$$\begin{array}{c|l|c|c|c|c|c|c|c} & & \text{Mass concentration of ion, } \mathrm{mg\,dm^{-3}} & & & & & & \\ \text{No.} & \text{Trade brand} & \ce{Ca^{2+}} & \ce{Mg^{2+}} & \ce{Na+} & \ce{K+} & \ce{Cl-} & \ce{SO4^{2-}} & \ce{HCO3-} \\ \hline 1 & \text{Kláštorná} & 290 & 74 & 71 & 16 & 15 & 89 & 1\,341 \\ 2 & \text{Budišská} & 200 & 50 & 445 & 50 & 25 & 433 & 1\,535 \\ 3 & \text{Baldovská} & 378 & 94 & 90 & 0 & 78 & 215 & 1\,557 \\ 4 & \text{Santovka} & 215 & 67 & 380 & 45 & 177 & 250 & 1\,462 \\ 5 & \text{Slatina} & 100 & 45 & 166 & 40 & 104 & 168 & 653 \\ 6 & \text{Fatra} & 45 & 48 & 550 & 16 & 36 & 111 & 1\,693 \\ 7 & \text{Ľubovnianka} & 152 & 173 & 174 & 5 & 10 & 20 & 1\,739 \\ 8 & \text{Gemerka} & 376 & 115 & 85 & 0 & 30 & 257 & 1\,532 \\ 9 & \text{Salvator} & 473 & 161 & 214 & 30 & 116 & 124 & 2\,585 \\ 10 & \text{Brusnianka} & 305 & 101 & 187 & 35 & 59 & 774 & 884 \\ 11 & \text{Maxia} & 436 & 136 & 107 & 18 & 37 & 379 & 1\,715 \end{array}$$

Notes:
• Use the prescribed symbols in the notations of calculations.
• You are provided with a swollen cation exchange resin (Catex) in its $\ce{H+}$ form. Use a thick stem Pasteur pipette for transferring it. You can add more deionized water to the resin if necessary (it should not dry out).
• Concentrations of the standard solutions: $c(\ce{NaOH}) = 0.2660\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, $c(\text{EDTA}) = 5.965\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$

Procedure

1.a Measure 5.00 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the catex into the graduated cylinder (volume $V1$). Then using deionized water transfer the catex quantitatively into a titration flask. Add an appropriate amount of deionized water so that the suspension can be swirled well and the colour of the solution over the catex can be observed.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/icx-2018-3-fig1.png

1.b Add 3–4 drops of the bromothymol blue indicator (BTB) and about 1 g (half a spoon) of solid NaCl. When NaCl dissolves, titrate all the suspension with the standard sodium hydroxide solution (volume $V2$) from yellow to blue. Close to the equivalence point, titrate slowly and swirl well so that any analyte inside the catex skeleton may diffuse into the solution. Repeat the experiment as necessary.

1.c After the titration, decant and discard most of the aqueous solution in the titration flask above the catex and transfer the suspension to the Waste catex container.

(You do not need to fill in all the rows.)

$$\begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Analysis No.} & \text{Catex volume } V1\ [\mathrm{cm^3}] & \text{NaOH consumption } V2\ [\mathrm{cm^3}] \\ \hline 1 & & \\ 2 & 5.00 & \\ 3 & & \\ \hline \text{Accepted value } V2\text{, 4 significant figures} & & \end{array}$$

2.a Using a graduated cylinder, measure 5.00 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of the swollen catex (volume $V3$). Transfer the measured catex quantitatively into the 250 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ beaker. 2.b Using deionized water, transfer the catex quantitatively from the funnel into a titration flask and discard the filtrate.

(You do not need to fill in all the rows.)

Add some Eriochrome black T indicator (EBT, on the tip of the spatula) and titrate with the standard EDTA solution from wine red to blue ($V7$).
